title: Microsoft's New AI Chip Could Change the Economics of AI - The Globe and Mail
description:
Its new Maia 300 chip is a clear sign and a potential catalyst ahead of earnings.
It expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.
Beyond Maia: Physical AI Is a Future Catalyst Physical AI, especially humanoid robots, is a later catalyst.
What Investors Should Watch in Microsoft's Upcoming Earnings Analysts expect earnings per share (EPS) of about $4.72 on revenue of $90.6 billion.
While Maia 300 won't begin deployment until 2027, it could eventually help Microsoft manage the costs of its expanding AI infrastructure.
text:
Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) wants to stop renting its AI future from NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA). Its new Maia 300 chip is a clear sign and a potential catalyst ahead of earnings.

Microsoft plans to deploy Maia chips at a multi-gigawatt scale starting in 2027. It expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.

More importantly, Microsoft says Maia will become the primary inference hardware for Microsoft’s own products. That speaks to the question hanging over every AI stock: Is this a bubble?

The bear case is simple. Generative AI is becoming a commodity. Chatbots are interchangeable, and token prices keep falling. Agentic AI may follow the same path. If the product is a commodity, why spend hundreds of billions on data centers?

Falling token prices don't necessarily mean weaker demand. Cheaper tokens can encourage more AI use, especially as agents take on increasingly complex tasks. Commodity markets don’t punish everyone equally, though. They reward the low-cost producer. Maia 300 is Microsoft’s attempt to become that producer.

Investors will get a fresh read on the strategy soon. Microsoft is estimated to report first-quarter fiscal year 2027 (FY2027) results after the close on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Maia 300 Targets the Real Constraint: Power

Electricity availability is becoming a major constraint on data center growth, even as demand increases. That makes tokens per megawatt an important measure of efficiency.

Maia 300's compute chiplets are built on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s (NYSE: TSM) N2P process, and the chip includes eight stacks of HBM4 memory. A full rack holds 96 chips. Microsoft says that a full rack delivers up to seven times the token throughput of a Maia 200 rack.

The chip targets long-context reasoning and multi-step agentic tasks. In other words, it was built for the workloads driving demand today.

Greater efficiency could allow Microsoft to process more AI workloads without a proportional increase in power consumption, potentially improving margins as usage grows.

The scale is meaningful, too. Reuters, citing The Information, reported that Microsoft ultimately aimed to secure manufacturing capacity for more than one million Maia 300 chips, although the company has not confirmed production targets. Microsoft plans to discuss its broader AI strategy at its Ignite conference in November.

Beyond Maia: Physical AI Is a Future Catalyst

Physical AI, especially humanoid robots, is a later catalyst. Counterpoint expects global humanoid shipments to top 50,000 units in 2026. That’s small next to agentic demand. But as adoption grows, robotics could create another source of demand for cloud-based AI services.

Microsoft won’t build robots. Instead, it’s positioning itself as the platform that trains, hosts and manages them. In January, Microsoft Research unveiled Rho-alpha, a robotics model that translates natural-language commands into robotic movements and incorporates tactile sensing. Microsoft plans to offer it through its Foundry platform.

The company also partnered with Hexagon Robotics in January to develop industrial humanoid applications, targeting automotive, aerospace, manufacturing, and logistics customers. Azure supports the cloud infrastructure behind that effort.

Here’s the link to Maia. Robot training and simulation already use cloud computing, while some inference happens on the robot itself. However, Microsoft is also exploring ways to shift inference workloads to edge and cloud infrastructure. If that approach gains traction, Maia's efficiency improvements could eventually help Microsoft serve those workloads at a lower cost.

Microsoft has not announced plans to use Maia for robotics, so the connection remains a possibility rather than an established use case. None of this will show up in the upcoming results. It’s optionality. But it gives Microsoft a potential second demand curve after AI agents.

Microsoft Stock Nears Highs as Analysts See More Upside

Microsoft’s chart shows MSFT in recovery mode. Shares rebounded from a midyear low and moved higher following the company's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings beat. After a strong rally in recent months, MSFT is trading near its 52-week high.

Momentum is constructive but not stretched. The Relative Strength Index (RSI) remains below overbought territory, while the MACD line remains above its signal line. Volume on the recent climb is lighter than during the August breakout. That’s worth watching into earnings.

Analysts remain supportive. MarketBeat-tracked analysts give MSFT a Moderate Buy consensus rating and an average price target of approximately $590, suggesting additional upside from recent levels.

What Investors Should Watch in Microsoft's Upcoming Earnings

Analysts expect earnings per share (EPS) of about $4.72 on revenue of $90.6 billion. Last quarter, Microsoft posted adjusted EPS of $4.74, beating the $4.24 estimate.

Azure growth will get most of the attention. Listen closely to the capital expenditure commentary, too. While Maia 300 won't begin deployment until 2027, it could eventually help Microsoft manage the costs of its expanding AI infrastructure. For now, investors will be looking for signs that Azure growth and profitability can justify the company's substantial spending.

text:
Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam’s Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.

The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.

“We’re giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships,” Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. “For $120 a year, we’re raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own.”

The membership gives customers access to Sam’s Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam’s Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.

While Walmart’s customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam’s Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.

The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.

In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.

Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it’s well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.

Meanwhile, Sam’s Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.

The membership business — which is part of Walmart’s push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam’s Club, that revenue number grew 6%.

Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.

The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company’s fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

description:

text:
Philly’s life sciences community is seeing wins this fall, including a major deal for a local startup.

Digital pathology company Proscia agreed to be acquired by Agilent Technologies for $240 million.

Plus, the Small Business Administration selected the Science Center for a $1 million grant to connect biomanufacturing resources in the region.

Other sectors within Philly’s tech community are also seeing financial support. The Pew Center for Arts and Heritage donated $90,000 to a gaming exhibit at Drexel University this fall.

Scroll down for all the details and more Money Moves.

Agilent to acquire Proscia in $240M deal

Local digital pathology company Proscia last week announced that it entered a definitive agreement to be acquired by global lab technology company Agilent Technologies.

The deal is worth $240 million in cash, with the potential for an additional $30 million if certain milestones are met.

Until the deal closes in fiscal year 2027, it’s too early to say exactly how Proscia’s approximately 100-person team will mesh with Agilent, according to David West, cofounder and CEO of Proscia. However, the acquisition is just as much about merging products and market presence as it is about talent.

“We’ve got a great nucleus of talent here,” West told Technical.ly. “We’ve also got people all over the world. We’re going to continue looking for great talent in Philly, and creating a culture that is great for our people here.”

Proscia and Agilent had an existing relationship, including a 2022 distribution agreement that combined their products to create a new diagnostic pathology system, West said. Agilent develops lab instruments for diagnostics, while Proscia provides software to support those tools.

“We’re going from this partnership model to [being] a part of the same company,” West said. “That gives us more scale, allows us to execute faster and also brings different capabilities that we don’t have.”

The timing of the move made sense because of both the state of the industry and Proscia’s scale, West said. The company had hit revenue goals that made it attractive to companies like Agilent.

Over the last decade, scientists and healthcare workers have become more open to digital pathology. Advances in AI and drug development make Proscia’s tech more enticing, he added.

West founded Proscia in 2014 as a biomedical engineering student at Johns Hopkins University. The company moved from Baltimore to Philly in 2018 to access more talent, West previously said.

Science Center gets $1M to launch biomanufacturing cluster

The Science Center received $1 million from the US Small Business Administration (SBA) to establish the Mid-Atlantic Biomanufacturing Scale-Up Cluster.

The money will support the Science Center’s programming related to the industry, which uses microorganisms or cells to grow or make products. The effort will connect related resources in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and DC.

“We’re really looking to navigate the biomanufacturing ecosystem on behalf of businesses to help them more readily access what is already there,” Heath Naquin, senior vice president of innovation and new ventures at the Science Center, told Technical.ly.

The initiative will be similar to its Capital Readiness Program, which prepares startup founders for fundraising. Funding from the SBA will support the Science Center’s efforts to educate early-stage companies about what they need to do to get ready for manufacturing and connect them with experts in the space.

The cluster will also help midsize companies make connections in the domestic manufacturing sector, according to Naquin.

Programs will be open to companies from across the country. The Science Center is focused on drawing attention to resources in the Greater Philadelphia region and creating lasting economic development opportunities, Naquin said.

“If we’re able to help, in some way, bring a company from wherever to establish their biomanufacturing facilities here,” Naquin said, “that goes to create jobs, that goes to create other things, that’s a win.”

This funding comes from the SBA’s Regional Innovation Clusters program, which selected nine orgs across the country this cycle to receive grants totaling more than $7 million. The sectors range widely from defense to transportation, aiming to connect entrepreneurs with applicable resources.

Drexel opens interactive gaming exhibit with $90k grant

A new video game-focused exhibit opened at Drexel University last week thanks to a $90,000 grant from the Pew Center for Arts and Heritage.

The interactive exhibit features games and displays from artists, historians and designers that explore the culture and community around gaming, co-organizer Christopher Grant told Technical.ly.

“Having a space to enjoy and share in what is often a very isolated hobby or isolated interest,” Grant said, “being able to share that in person with people is just very unusual.”

Some of the exhibit’s displays include a timeline of queer gaming history put together by local Temple University and Drexel professors and a virtual reality experience based on Taiwan’s period of martial law.

The group aims to challenge people’s existing ideas about gaming.

“Especially for folks who maybe don’t think of it as something that would fit into a traditional art gallery,” Grant said, “that they might be pressured to reexamine that bias and why they think of it.”

title: Albertsons begins its $8B trial against Kroger over failed merger - Idaho Business Review
description:
The bench trial is scheduled to run two weeks in Delaware’s Court of Chancery in front of Vice Chancellor Lori Will.
In December 2024, federal and state courts blocked the deal and Albertsons immediately terminated the merger, which Ohio-based Kroger said cut off its ability to appeal.
Kroger said in its court papers Albertsons was misreading the merger agreement and said that it kept its obligations, pinning the deal failure on regulatory opposition.
Kroger said it will prove at the trial that Albertsons isn’t entitled to the termination fee because it claims Albertsons undermined Kroger’s ability to negotiate.
Dozens of other potential witnesses include deal advisers, expert witnesses and current and former executives and directors.
text:
WILMINGTON, DEL.―Grocery chain Albertsons Companies will begin making its case in court on Monday for more than $8 billion in damages against larger rival Kroger for allegedly sinking their agreed $24.6 billion merger two years ago.

Boise-based Albertsons, whose chains include Safeway, Acme and Kings Food Markets, claims that Kroger broke its commitment to obtain regulatory approval for the deal by refusing to sell a sufficient number of stores. As a result, Albertsons said it is owed a premium of up to $6.88 billion the deal would have delivered to its shareholders, as well as the $600 million termination fee and more than $1 billion in tax adjustments.

The bench trial is scheduled to run two weeks in Delaware’s Court of Chancery in front of Vice Chancellor Lori Will. Rulings often take months after the trial ends and the outcome can be appealed to the Delaware Supreme Court.

The 2022 merger was meant to position the two companies and their 5,000 stores to better compete with newer entrants into grocery markets such as Walmart, Costco, Amazon and Aldi.

However, combining the largest and second-largest U.S. grocers was challenged by states and the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden, which argued the deal would remove direct competition and lead to higher prices at checkout.

In December 2024, federal and state courts blocked the deal and Albertsons immediately terminated the merger, which Ohio-based Kroger said cut off its ability to appeal.

Since the termination, Kroger’s stock has risen about 4% and Albertsons has lost nearly 30%, both lagging the S&P 500 index, which rose by more than a quarter.

The trial comes a week after Albertsons unveiled a cost-cutting review of its business and after Kroger, which owns the Dillons, Ralphs and Fred Meyer chains, planned to cut 3,000 jobs and invest in technology to lower prices.

Albertsons said that Kroger violated what it claimed was an obligation to take “any and all actions” to get antitrust approval, up to selling 650 stores.

Albertsons described in court papers the various divestiture packages that Kroger offered regulators as an attempt to minimize what it had to sell to protect the profitability of the post-merger business, rather than to get regulatory clearance.

It said Kroger created a $400 million executive bonus pool to encourage senior managers to take a highly aggressive approach to demands from regulators.

Kroger said in its court papers Albertsons was misreading the merger agreement and said that it kept its obligations, pinning the deal failure on regulatory opposition. It said that the Biden administration wanted it to sell more than 650 stores and courts blocked the merger because they took a narrow view of the grocery market by excluding Amazon, Costco and others.

Albertsons CEO could be witness

Kroger spent more than $1 billion and tens of thousands of hours of employee and adviser time trying to close the deal, which it said was evidence it was not willfully breaching the merger agreement.

Kroger said it will prove at the trial that Albertsons isn’t entitled to the termination fee because it claims Albertsons undermined Kroger’s ability to negotiate. It blamed that in part on allegedly unauthorized communications about the divestment plan by Susan Morris, who is now Albertsons’ CEO. Albertsons said there is zero evidence Morris shared sensitive information.

In addition to Morris, other potential witnesses include Rodney McMullen and Vivek Sankaran, who were CEOs of Kroger and Albertsons respectively at the time of the merger but who have since been replaced, according to court documents.

Dozens of other potential witnesses include deal advisers, expert witnesses and current and former executives and directors.

Reporting by Tom Hals in Wilmington, Delaware; Editing by Cynthia Osterman.

name: Walmart
title: Walmart's Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India | TechCrunch
description:
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy.
Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market.
Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market.
Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it.
Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.
text:
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in.

The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch.

The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms, as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly.

Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered.

As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions.

Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing, a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay.

“Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.”

Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms.

Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru, but it shut the service down two years later. Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato.

Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.

“Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch.

Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy.

Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order.

Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them.

Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. The company has told restaurants that it expects to launch its food-delivery service publicly by the end of October and to expand to five or six cities by the end of this year, Daryani told TechCrunch.

The food-delivery push also comes as Flipkart’s long-awaited stock-market listing remains uncertain. Chief Executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above) recently declined to give a timetable for an IPO, even as the company continues to expand into businesses that could bring customers back to its app more frequently.

Flipkart’s expansion comes as competition in India’s e-commerce market intensifies. Quick-commerce platforms that started by delivering groceries in minutes now sell even the latest iPhones and other discretionary purchases, putting them in more direct competition with Flipkart and Amazon.

Flipkart did not respond to a request for comments.

description:
Highlights Ananth Chandramouli takes charge of Capgemini’s Insights & Data business across Asia Pacific and the Middle East.
The regional business will focus on scaling data, analytics and AI capabilities to deliver measurable enterprise outcomes.
Capgemini Expands Regional Data and AI Leadership Capgemini has elevated Ananth Chandramouli to Executive Vice President and Managing Director of Insights & Data for Asia Pacific and the Middle East.
From India Business Leadership to a Regional Mandate During his tenure leading Capgemini’s India business, Chandramouli oversaw business strategy, revenue growth, client relationships and operations.
Capgemini’s regional Insights & Data business brings together services and capabilities spanning data management, analytics, AI and enterprise transformation.
text:
Highlights

Ananth Chandramouli takes charge of Capgemini’s Insights & Data business across Asia Pacific and the Middle East.

He previously led Capgemini’s India business for more than nine years.

His new remit covers markets including India, Southeast Asia, China, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and the Middle East.

Chandramouli brings more than two decades of experience at Infosys, spanning technology consulting, solutions architecture and client leadership.

The regional business will focus on scaling data, analytics and AI capabilities to deliver measurable enterprise outcomes.

Capgemini Expands Regional Data and AI Leadership

Capgemini has elevated Ananth Chandramouli to Executive Vice President and Managing Director of Insights & Data for Asia Pacific and the Middle East. In his new role, he will lead the regional business responsible for helping enterprise clients develop and scale data, analytics and artificial intelligence capabilities.

The appointment expands Chandramouli’s responsibilities beyond his previous position as Executive Vice President and Managing Director of Capgemini’s India business, which he led for more than nine years. His new remit spans diverse markets, including India, Southeast Asia, China, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and the Middle East.

The move comes as enterprises increasingly look to turn AI experimentation into measurable business results. Organisations are investing in data platforms, analytics and AI-enabled workflows, but scaling these technologies requires more than deploying individual models. Businesses also need reliable data foundations, industry-specific expertise, technology integration and the ability to execute transformation programmes across complex operations.

Chandramouli’s appointment places an experienced business and technology leader at the head of Capgemini’s regional Insights & Data operations as the company works with clients on these challenges.

From India Business Leadership to a Regional Mandate

During his tenure leading Capgemini’s India business, Chandramouli oversaw business strategy, revenue growth, client relationships and operations. The role involved managing commercial priorities and strengthening relationships with enterprise customers across a major technology-services market.

That experience provides a business-management foundation for his expanded regional responsibilities. Across Asia Pacific and the Middle East, organisations differ in their digital maturity, regulatory environments, industry requirements and approaches to AI adoption. Regional leadership must therefore balance common technology capabilities with the needs of individual markets and clients.

Capgemini’s regional Insights & Data business brings together services and capabilities spanning data management, analytics, AI and enterprise transformation. Its challenge is to help customers connect these capabilities to practical business objectives rather than pursue technology adoption in isolation.

In a LinkedIn announcement, Chandramouli emphasised the importance of combining data and AI capabilities with strong data foundations, industry context and the ability to execute transformation at scale. He also identified the company’s technology partner ecosystem as part of its approach to helping clients develop enterprise-ready solutions.

More Than Two Decades of Experience at Infosys

Before joining Capgemini, Chandramouli spent more than 20 years at Infosys in roles covering technology consulting, client services, solutions architecture and business development.

His experience included leadership responsibilities across industries such as manufacturing, retail, telecommunications and energy. He also worked in enterprise architecture and solutions development, helping organisations address technology strategy and complex IT requirements.

This combination of technical and commercial experience is relevant to enterprise AI programmes, which often require coordination among technology teams, business stakeholders and service providers. Organisations must identify suitable use cases, prepare the underlying data, integrate systems and establish ways to evaluate whether deployments produce meaningful results.

Chandramouli’s career progression from technology-focused responsibilities to business leadership reflects the increasingly close relationship between enterprise technology strategy and commercial outcomes.

Scaling Enterprise AI Beyond Experimentation

A central challenge for companies adopting AI is moving from isolated proofs of concept to systems that can operate reliably across business functions. That transition involves data quality, governance, integration with existing platforms, security and the redesign of workflows.

Capgemini has identified data foundations and industry expertise as important elements of its approach. Its regional business can draw on capabilities and assets including Syniti, Bionic Foundry and RAISE, alongside its ecosystem of technology partners, according to Chandramouli’s announcement.

These capabilities form part of a broader services landscape in which enterprises combine consulting, data engineering, analytics and AI implementation. The commercial objective is to connect technology investments to outcomes such as improved decision-making, more efficient processes and new digital services.

However, results depend on the circumstances of each client engagement. The appointment does not, by itself, establish specific revenue targets, new AI product launches or deployment commitments for the regional business.

Implications for Asia Pacific and the Middle East

Chandramouli’s expanded role brings together markets at different stages of data and AI adoption under one regional leadership structure. India remains an important technology and enterprise-services market, while organisations across the Middle East and Asia Pacific are pursuing their own digital transformation priorities.

For Capgemini, the opportunity is to combine regional scale with market-specific expertise and help clients progress from experimentation to implementation. The next phase will depend on how effectively its teams translate technology capabilities into solutions suited to customers’ operational and commercial needs.

The appointment therefore represents both a leadership transition and a wider strategic focus on enterprise data and AI. Its significance will ultimately be measured by the regional business’s ability to help clients scale these capabilities and demonstrate tangible business value.

title: Rich flyers' splurges are saving airlines from a margin collapse - The Business Times
description:

United Airlines, American Airlines and Southwest appear likely to offer similarly tepid forecasts later this week.
Delta’s recent revamp of its Delta One business class includes wagyu burgers, Blanton’s single-barrel bourbon, Champagne Taittinger and wines that can retail for more than US$200 a bottle.
British Airways’ retrofit of its double-decker Airbus A380s later this year will offer more business class seats to capture the “very resilient” demand for premium travel, IAG CEO Luis Gallego said.

text:
ROBERT Doornbos spent more on flights in 2025 than the average American earns annually, but the retired Formula 1 driver said that doing so was his way of buying back time.

Doornbos, who lives in Dubai, said he took about 50 flights last year in business class. He has been willing to stomach higher airfares – like the 7,500 euros (US$8,407) he shelled out for a ticket to Madrid to attend a Grand Prix – for the comfort of arriving rested and ready to work.

“I try to minimise the time loss,” said Doornbos, who now works as a public speaker. “Lots of flying, but in an efficient way.”

Doornbos is exactly the kind of customer the world’s biggest airlines have in mind as they push ever deeper into luxury travel, betting that affluent passengers will continue splurging on expensive seats even as airfares soar.

Just in the last few weeks, British Airways introduced the biggest business class cabin anywhere in the market; Delta Air Lines said it was almost doubling its fleet of Porsche cars shuttling loyal customers from plane to airport building; and even the once frugally minded Southwest Airlines is adding premium options.

US airline ticket prices jumped 22 per cent in September from a year earlier, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Yet, executives say demand for their priciest seats has hardly wavered, even as more budget-conscious travellers face increasing pressure.

“When you look at the top 40 per cent of our customer base, they’ve accumulated over US$40 trillion of wealth over the last few years,” Delta CEO Ed Bastian said in an interview ahead of the carrier’s third-quarter earnings results.

“They have the means, they’re prioritising travel, and it’s high on their list.”

Consumer demand is providing a crucial lifeline for an industry grappling with rising fuel costs and lower profit margins as a result of the US-Iran war, which is showing no signs of abating.

Analysts expect energy prices to remain elevated, prolonging the financial strain of carriers around the globe. US President Donald Trump has said the fighting could end after the November midterm elections.

Underlying business is strong, airlines say, but high fuel prices are hurting their bottom lines.

Delta, one of the industry’s best performers, recently cut its full-year earnings outlook. United Airlines, American Airlines and Southwest appear likely to offer similarly tepid forecasts later this week.

How the turnaround is unfolding

Delta said that, for the first time in commercial aviation history, its quarterly premium ticket revenue surpassed traditional main cabin sales, with premium demand unabating.

Eric Gentry, 65, the co-founder of Jet Set Natural, a herbal supplement to treat jet lag, accepts higher fares because travel is among his favourite ways to spend his free time. He has travelled to Mexico City, Sicily and South Carolina in just the past year.

“If the air travel is significantly increased, you may scale back a little bit on the other end with hotels, accommodations and what you’ll be doing there,” he said. “You have to get there one way or another. So if you want to get to a destination, you absorb the pricing.”

Airlines are pouring investment into their most lucrative cabins, transforming what was once a comfortable way to travel into something resembling a luxury hotel at 35,000 feet.

Delta’s recent revamp of its Delta One business class includes wagyu burgers, Blanton’s single-barrel bourbon, Champagne Taittinger and wines that can retail for more than US$200 a bottle.

The carrier is also introducing Missoni pillows and expanding its fleet of Porsche vehicles for premium airport transfers.

Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s chief marketing and product officer, said that “consistent investment in premium experiences is so important because customers have choices, and no matter what the environment is, you have to win the day and win the wallet".

Premiumisation around the world

The obsession with the front of the plane extends beyond the US.

British Airways’ retrofit of its double-decker Airbus A380s later this year will offer more business class seats to capture the “very resilient” demand for premium travel, IAG CEO Luis Gallego said.

Rival Air France-KLM recently won an award for having the world’s best first class in Skytrax’s annual airline rankings.

The rush of upscaling cabins has affected some carriers, including Deutsche Lufthansa, which faced certification delays on its Allegris seats, forcing the airline to fly new Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft with largely cordoned off business class areas.

“In the past, economy class would sell out first because people prioritised price, leaving first and business class seats available just days before departure,” Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr said at a media gathering.

“Now, it is the other way around: First, business, and premium economy sell out first.”

Even Southwest, long known for its no-frills approach, is chasing higher-paying customers. Tony Roach, the carrier’s chief customer and brand officer, told Bloomberg on Oct 15 that “adding premium options is about broadening its appeal rather than abandoning its traditional customer base”.

“Travel,” he said, “is a passion point.”

Adding to the frenzy, Bastian and other CEOs have said that higher airfares will not deter people who love to travel.

Gentry is one of those customers. He is in the middle of planning a trip somewhere warm for a beach holiday, and has made some concessions: He opted for Miami instead of the Caribbean because it was a bit cheaper.

He is flexible with the destination, he said, but the trip itself is the priority.

“I don’t think I’m gonna travel less,” he said. “What I’ll do is budget accordingly, especially if I wanna keep the frequency of travel.” BLOOMBERG

title: Icotrokinra's NEJM Data Reveals the Quiet Shift in How UC Trials Get Designed and Approved
description:

That last point matters operationally: Phase 2b trials in UC have increasingly absorbed the evidentiary burden that regulators once accepted from Phase 3 interim analyses.
That assumption is wrong, and it misreads what the NEJM data actually signals about where the trial design pressure is now concentrated.
It is about whether the Phase 2b data package is granular enough to support a single-dose pivotal without generating a Complete Response Letter asking for additional dose-ranging data.
For sites, the icotrokinra NEJM publication creates an enrollment environment that cuts both ways.
text:
Three forces converged in the October 15, 2026 issue of the New England Journal of Medicine with enough quiet force that most clinical operations teams will miss the signal entirely. The publication of Johnson & Johnson’s Phase 2 trial of icotrokinra for ulcerative colitis,, marks more than a positive readout for a single drug. It marks a convergence point: a new molecular class, a design architecture that reflects the FDA’s current evidentiary preferences, and a publication strategy that signals exactly where Johnson & Johnson intends to anchor its regulatory narrative going forward.

The stakes are immediate. Icotrokinra, a targeted oral peptide that selectively blocks the IL-23 receptor, met its primary endpoint of clinical response across all dose groups in the Phase 2b ANTHEM-UC study, the trial that established the foundation for this NEJM publication. Protagonist Therapeutics discovered the molecule; J&J took over development and commercialization, with the product branded as ICOTYDE™. What gets buried under the commercial narrative is the design infrastructure that made the data credible enough to land in the NEJM in the first place, and that infrastructure carries operational lessons the industry needs to absorb now.

The Design Signal Inside the Data

Read the FDA’s draft guidance on ulcerative colitis drug development closely enough and a specific mandate emerges: for induction trials, clinical remission, defined as a modified Mayo score of 0 to 2 with no individual subscore exceeding 1, should serve as the primary endpoint. That FDA framework for IBD drug development is not merely a recommendation sitting in a PDF. It functions as a design constraint, and sponsors who treat it as optional do so at the cost of their own Phase 3 readiness.

The ANTHEM-UC Phase 2b structure reflects exactly this constraint. Modified Mayo scoring anchored the endpoint architecture, clinical response drove the primary readout, and the dose-ranging across all groups gave the sponsor the flexibility to make a defensible dose selection argument before entering the Phase 3 investment. That last point matters operationally: Phase 2b trials in UC have increasingly absorbed the evidentiary burden that regulators once accepted from Phase 3 interim analyses. The NEJM publication of this data is not incidental to J&J’s regulatory strategy. It is the strategy.

Publishing Phase 2b results in the NEJM before Phase 3 completion does something that a sponsor cannot achieve through FDA briefing documents alone: it socializes the efficacy signal with the clinical community that will eventually enroll Phase 3 patients, run the sites, and interpret the package insert. When investigators read a positive Phase 2 readout in the journal they trust most, site activation timelines compress. Principal investigators do not need to be sold on a hypothesis that already has an NEJM imprimatur.

Where the Pattern Gets Uncomfortable

Here is the assumption most clinical operations teams are currently making: the icotrokinra readout confirms that IL-23 receptor blockade works in UC, and the operational challenge is simply running a clean Phase 3 to replicate it. That assumption is wrong, and it misreads what the NEJM data actually signals about where the trial design pressure is now concentrated.

The counterintuitive reality is that a clean Phase 2b with strong dose-response data across all groups creates a different kind of Phase 3 problem: the FDA now expects sponsors to have solved dose selection before they file the IND for the pivotal study. When every dose group in Phase 2b hits clinical response, the sponsor faces a dose-selection argument that must be made on durability, safety profile, and patient-reported outcomes rather than on efficacy discrimination. That argument requires endpoint architecture in Phase 2b that most UC programs did not build because they expected dose selection to be straightforward. The Phase 3 design conversation is no longer about whether the drug works. It is about whether the Phase 2b data package is granular enough to support a single-dose pivotal without generating a Complete Response Letter asking for additional dose-ranging data.

Sponsors running UC programs behind J&J should look at the icotrokinra ANTHEM-UC design not as a template to replicate, but as an evidentiary bar being set in real time.

The Operational Ripple for Sponsors, CROs, and Sites

For sponsors, the ANTHEM-UC publication compresses timelines in one direction while expanding complexity in another. The NEJM signal accelerates competitive pressure in the IL-23 space: any sponsor running a Phase 2 UC program right now is being measured against a published dataset, not a hypothetical. That changes how data monitoring committees frame interim reviews, how medical affairs teams pitch Phase 3 enrollment, and how CFOs think about the investment case for the next milestone payment.

For CROs managing UC trial operations, the operational implication runs through endpoint adjudication infrastructure. Modified Mayo scoring requires central reading of endoscopy data, and central reading quality has become an area of increasing regulatory attention in IBD submissions. The FDA’s guidance on UC drug development explicitly ties clinical remission definitions to endoscopic subscores, which means that any variability in central reader training or grading consistency becomes a data integrity issue with direct regulatory consequence, not merely a protocol deviation to be explained in the clinical study report. CROs that invested in central reading platforms and reader qualification programs before this publication now hold a structural advantage in winning Phase 3 operational mandates from sponsors who need to move fast.

For sites, the icotrokinra NEJM publication creates an enrollment environment that cuts both ways. Strong published efficacy data attracts patients and referring physicians, which supports screen rates. But strong published Phase 2b data also raises the evidentiary bar for placebo arm participation: patients who have read or been told about icotrokinra’s performance in ANTHEM-UC will ask harder questions about placebo assignment probability, and site staff need to be prepared for that conversation in the informed consent process. Retention, not just recruitment, becomes the operational pressure point in the Phase 3 population that forms after a high-profile Phase 2 publication.

Technology vendors operating in eCOA and ePRO should pay attention to one specific consequence: if modified Mayo scoring anchors the FDA’s preferred endpoint architecture for UC induction trials, then any electronic patient-reported outcome platform that cannot support Mayo stool frequency and rectal bleeding subscores with validated data capture faces a significant barrier to qualification for Phase 3 UC programs. That is not a future market dynamic. Given the ANTHEM-UC timeline and J&J’s Phase 3 trajectory with icotrokinra, vendor qualification decisions are being made now.

The broader pattern that the ANTHEM-UC publication confirms is one the industry has been watching form across therapeutic areas without naming it directly: the NEJM as regulatory pre-positioning tool. High-profile journal publication before Phase 3 IND filing is no longer a coincidence of scientific timing. It is a deliberate sequencing choice that shapes investigator enthusiasm, patient awareness, competitive intelligence, and the FDA review team’s familiarity with the dataset before the NDA lands. J&J executed this sequence with precision on icotrokinra. The sponsors who recognize this as a replicable strategic pattern, rather than a J&J-specific advantage, will build it into their Phase 2b publication timelines for every pivotal-track program. Those who treat it as background noise will find themselves explaining to Phase 3 site investigators why their data has not been published anywhere.

If a sponsor files a Phase 3 UC IND whose Phase 2b data the FDA review team has already encountered through a major journal publication, it may begin to shift how evidentiary credibility is established before a single pivotal patient is enrolled. The icotrokinra program has already started that clock.

(Adds dropped words in headline and first paragraph to clarify UniCredit is repurchasing its own local business)

MILAN, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Italy's second-biggest bank, UniCredit, has signed an agreement to repurchase its domestic securities-services business from French peer Societe Generale, according to a union document seen by Reuters on Monday.

The unit, which looks after investors' securities and handles related administrative services, has 54 staff in Milan and Turin, according to the document, which did not provide any financial details of the agreement.

Societe Generale bought UniCredit's securities services unit in 2006, striking a long-term partnership to handle those services for the Italian bank. The supply contract was last renewed in 2017 until 2026.

UniCredit is seeking to bring in-house activities it deems strategic, and the transaction is part of that effort, the document said.

Handling the securities itself will reduce the need for an external supplier and improve use of the business' data,

UniCredit and Societe Generale did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

text:
By Echo Wang, Krystal Hu and Sabrina Valle

NEW YORK, Oct 19 (Reuters) – OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over $1.4 trillion, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping in to a similar investor base, the people said, adding that OpenAI wants ​to capitalize on its recent revenue growth after launching new models. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round ‌of about $30 billion, one of the people said.

The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of AI valuations.

OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI’s funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said.

Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the IPO markets further delays its ‌planned 2027 ​listing.

Though there is high demand for the shares of both companies, investors face the challenge of evaluating and allocating capital to ⁠two complex, competing offerings within days or weeks of ⁠each other. Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO, the people said.

OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

TRYING TO HEAD OFF COMPARISONS

OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached $50 billion in annualized revenue and expecting that figure to rise to $70 billion by year-end, according to one of the people.

OpenAI has ​also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the person added.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached roughly $65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to $16.8 billion in the third quarter from $11.6 billion in the second quarter this year, it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth ⁠has raised concerns among investors about its valuation.

OpenAI is seeking to complete the fundraising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures ⁠give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said.

The disclosures could prompt investors to ​press OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company’s revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares ​upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier ‌that it follows established accounting practices.

“OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison),” said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. “It’s really a two-horse race in terms of being public.”

OpenAI was last valued at $852 billion in March this year, after a record-breaking $122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to $50 billion in the lab.

The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI’s potential fundraising.

IPO PLANS HIT BY ⁠MARKET JITTERS

A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic’s planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks, bankers and investors said. Some late-stage companies are also timing private fundraising rounds to avoid coinciding with Anthropic’s expected debut, the bankers and investors said.

Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued ⁠for a valuation closer to $1.5 trillion for its market debut — instead of ‌the desired $2 trillion — after the AI startup’s third-quarter results fell short of expectations, Reuters reported last week.

The reassessment comes amid a choppy ⁠market since September, with volatility in oil prices, rising bond yields and growing concerns about AI safety weighing on investor appetite for ​technology stocks. Investors ‌are also scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure, including the debt needed to finance the data centers powering the boom.

At the ​center of the latest ⁠concerns is cloud provider CoreWeave, whose shares and debt tumbled last week as investors scrutinized the nearly $50 billion in borrowings used to fund its rapid expansion.

The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans amid market volatility and concerns about valuations. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings.

Nuclear services company Holtec cited a “perfect storm,” driven mainly by uncertainty around data-center demand, when it pulled its US listing last month.

Companies in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, widely viewed as a proxy for AI-related semiconductor demand, have shed $1.6 trillion in less than two weeks, while AI infrastructure companies have come under particular pressure.

(Reporting by Echo Wang and Sabrina Valle in New York and Krystal Hu in San ​Francisco; Editing by Colin Barr and Matthew Lewis)

title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as 'frontier models can't be trusted'
description:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses.

OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
text:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

text:
Marinaro’s Expanded Responsibilities and Compensation Details at Medtronic

According to the filing, Medtronic plc’s Board of Directors approved Michael Marinaro’s appointment as President on October 15, 2026, effective October 14, 2026. In this expanded role, Marinaro will maintain oversight of the Medical Surgical Portfolio, Americas, and Global Commercial Operations, while also taking on responsibility for the company’s Greater China operations. These operations will continue to be locally managed by Alex Gu, Senior Vice President and President, Greater China. Marinaro will report directly to Geoffrey S. Martha, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer.

The Compensation and Talent Committee approved Marinaro’s $1,000,000 base salary for fiscal year 2027, with a target annual incentive opportunity of 100% under the Medtronic Incentive Plan. Supplemental long-term incentive awards totaling approximately $3.25 million will be granted on November 2, 2026, under the 2021 Medtronic plc Long-Term Incentive Plan. The $1.625 million performance share unit award will vest on April 27, 2029, based on performance from fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The $975,000 stock option award will vest in four equal annual installments starting August 3, 2027, with a ten-year term. The $650,000 restricted stock unit award will fully vest on August 3, 2029.

The filing also noted that as of the August 21, 2026 record date, 1,279,980,861 ordinary shares were outstanding and eligible to vote. At the Annual General Meeting, 1,116,484,432 shares were represented, establishing a quorum. Besides director elections and auditor ratification, shareholders approved renewing the Board’s authority to issue shares (1,100,821,210 votes for), to opt out of pre-emption rights under Irish law (1,036,661,831 votes for), and authorized overseas market purchases of Medtronic ordinary shares by the company or subsidiaries (1,081,959,682 votes for). The non-binding advisory vote on named executive officer compensation passed with 936,336,164 votes in favor.

Summary of Disclosures

Medtronic plc’s October 19, 2026 Form 8-K detailed Michael Marinaro’s appointment as President with updated compensation, full voting results from the October 15, 2026 Annual General Meeting covering six proposals, and the finalized separation of MiniMed Group, Inc.

text:
Subaru's European range is all Toyota-based EVs from 2028

Subaru will sell no combustion car in Europe after the end of 2027, and the three electric models that remain all sit on Toyota platforms. AutoNext reported last week that the boxer engine is leaving Europe model by model, which leaves the Solterra on the bZ4X, the E-Outback on the bZ4X Touring and the Uncharted on the C-HR+. Subaru's biggest electric car, the seven-seat Getaway, is a Toyota co-development as well. The Sano prototype is the first electric hardware in years that is Subaru's own underneath, and its roughly 2029 timing leaves European dealers selling Toyota-engineered cars alone for at least a year after the boxer goes.

Subaru promised 600,000 electric cars a year by 2030

In 2023 Subaru set a target of 600,000 battery-electric sales a year by 2030, half of its planned global volume, backed by 1.5 trillion yen of electrification spending. By November 2025 it had spent about 300 billion yen, put the remaining 1.2 trillion under review and said it was considering postponing the four in-house electric models it had scheduled by 2028. President Atsushi Osaki said it was appropriate to delay full-scale investment in EV mass production. The Sano mule is what survived that review: a platform, a battery and the electronics, without a launch date. Subaru built 878,016 cars worldwide in 2025, 6.4% fewer than a year earlier, which explains why it is spending carefully.

510 hp, under four seconds and a 100 kg lighter EV platform

Subaru's prototype makes 510 hp through all four wheels and reaches 100 km/h in under four seconds, and its motors are smaller and lighter than those in the brand's current EVs. The architecture targets a weight saving of 100 kg over the electric Subarus built today. The crash structure is new as well: supports curve over the front wheels to spread impact forces, and the front motor is designed to rotate in a collision so that it absorbs energy instead of pushing into the cabin or the battery. The body is an improvised development shell, so it says nothing about the shape of an eventual production car.

Panasonic's 4,000 cells and Aisin's motors power Subaru's in-house EV

The battery holds 4,000 cylindrical cells from Panasonic Energy, and Subaru says it weighs 25% less than its previous pack while aiming for an energy density 20% above the industry average. The drive units come from Aisin, a Toyota Group supplier, so the platform is a Subaru design rather than a Subaru parts list. Both partnerships were signed in March 2024, a week apart. Subaru has not given battery capacity, range or charging speed, which are the three figures a European buyer would compare first.

Subaru's own control unit runs on an AMD chip, not Toyota's Arene

Subaru is developing one integrated electronic control unit to run driver assistance, chassis, powertrain and infotainment from a chip co-designed with AMD. It brings over-the-air updates to a Subaru-developed car for the first time and will support AI functions in a future version of EyeSight. Subaru plans to build the unit itself and use it in electric, hybrid and petrol models alike, and has no current plan to adopt Toyota's Arene software, which Toyota expects to run in 10 million new cars a year by 2030. Its new methods also cut vehicle development time by about 40%, Subaru says.

AutoNext Take

Subaru is not leaving Toyota; it is taking back the parts of the car that make it a Subaru. Aisin still supplies the motors and Toyota still owns about a fifth of the company, but the structure, the crash engineering and the electronics that decide how all-wheel drive and EyeSight behave are now Subaru's own work. For a brand whose buyers chose it for traction and safety more than for an engine layout, that is the half of the car worth owning, and the Sano prototype shows Subaru can still engineer it.

The four in-house EVs promised for 2028 have already slipped once. Subaru's next big stage is the full Japan Mobility Show in autumn 2027, where it showed the Performance-E STI concept last time; if no production body for this platform appears there, no European Subaru built on it will arrive before 2030, and the gap after the boxer will stretch beyond two years.

name: Delta Airlines
title: Delta Just Unveiled Its Biggest Overhaul in 30 Years—Here's What It Means for Premium Travel
description: In a world of airlines stripping amenities to haul more and more passengers, Delta’s overhaul recognizes that luxury at altitude is not just about a seat that lays flat
text:
Summer 2026 is shaping up to be among the most expensive tra…

I have taken over 35 flights this year, so I consider myself…











Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines.

Woman sleeping with Missoni bedding and amenity kit in Delta One.

Once you’ve flown long-haul at 35,000 feet, you know that commercial air travel is often the furthest from comfort that one can get. Over the last decades, seats have gotten thinner, legroom has shrunk, hot meals have become bags of pretzels. We’ve learned to pack our own snacks and charge up our noise-canceling headphones because expectations are at an all-time low.

So, when a legacy airline announces its most significant cabin overhaul in nearly 30 years, many of us are curious what these luxury promises entail.

Delta Air Lines has officially pulled back the curtain on a multi-billion-dollar reimagining of its front-of-cabin experience, a total reset of the Delta One journey. Built on 20 years of gathered passenger feedback and backed by sweeping fleet investments, the new debut is bringing real comfort back to commercial air.

The redesign aims to restore the craft and hospitality that flights used to be known for, and it is scheduled to drop first on transoceanic routes before expanding across the carrier’s global network through early 2027.

Here is what flyers can expect.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

When Delta surveyed its highest-tier flyers about why they drop significant money on premium business class, the answer was overwhelmingly simple: getting good sleep. By angling the suites at 30 degrees toward the windows, designers unlocked three additional inches of bed length—creating an 81-inch lie-flat bed (six feet, eight inches) that comfortably accommodates almost any passenger.

Delta integrated a custom memory-foam cushion that wraps completely around the seat, topped with an additional Missoni-branded mattress pad. Touchpoint details abound: seat controls operate with a smooth, Mercedes-style tactile toggle, a dedicated button tilts the seat into a weight-distributing Zero-G position, and there are even built-in hooks specifically for purses and eyeglasses.

Their sleekest and tallest enclosed privacy doors yet, wireless charging, and mammoth 24-inch 4K QLED screens show their technological advances, plus a 50 times expansion in in-flight entertainment content, giving flyers thousands of titles to choose from.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

Delta’s culinary team wanted to elevate culinary craft, sourcing and consistency at altitude. To solve the notorious difficulty of serving restaurant-quality food in a low-pressure cabin environment, Delta brought in Michelin-starred Chef Simon Hulstone alongside Master Sommelier Andrea Robinson.

Every dish was re-engineered around altitude-proof physics. A mushroom risotto utilizes specially encapsulated Italian rice designed to withstand the humidity and reheat cycles of galley ovens. A 12-hour braised short rib is paired with a rich potato gratin and reduced jus, while a classic chicken breast is balanced with silky potato purée and roasted onions.

On international routes, regionally inspired menus feature Hong Kong-style sea bass from Chef Jereme Leung, authentic Japanese course dining curated by Chef Norio Ueno, and a custom Wagyu beef burger topped with caramelized onions and cornichons on a brioche bun.

To finish, a dessert cart featuring a dairy-free sorbet float with Champagne Taittinger and an ice cream sundae bar.

Drink options have also gotten a major boost. Bourbon collectors will spot Blanton’s Single Barrel on the cart starting this winter—a rare label rarely seen at altitude. The wine program, crafted with Andrea Robinson, who is an expert on how the palate receives wine at 35,000 feet, leans heavily into California icons like Napa Valley Cabernets and Sonoma Pinot Noirs alongside organic French Chablis. For lighter pours, Delta introduced a cocktail and mocktail lineup featuring alcoholic and zero-proof takes on the Hugo Spritz and Paloma.

Photo Credit: Delta Airlines

Passenger autonomy was also on the hit list of the new Delta One design team. Delta expanded its pre-select dining window up to 18 hours prior to departure, allowing travelers to lock in specialized choices—including gluten-free fare, lighter dishes, or pre-arrival plates designed specifically for those who want to maximize sleep and skip the full dinner service altogether.

Service itself features custom, heavy-gauge tableware and redesigned place settings that eliminate clutter on the console.

Partnering with Italian fashion house Missoni, Delta is introducing Winter Elsewhere amenity kits packed with Grown Alchemist skincare, a Marvis dental kit, and Missoni eye masks. On ultra-long-haul routes, a second Missoni Mini pillow joins the bedding setup for enhanced neck support, while cushioned Bombas socks return to keep feet warm during transit.

Even ground connections are expanding: Delta’s signature tarmac transfer program—where select passengers are met on the runway and whisked directly to their next gate—is expanding its fleet of Porsche hybrid vehicles from 40 to 70 across 15 major hubs by 2028.

In a world of airlines stripping amenities to haul more and more passengers, Delta’s overhaul recognizes that luxury at altitude is not just about a seat that lays flat; it’s about hot, Michelin-worthy meals with fresh cracked pepper, a wine that sits well in the mouth at altitude, customizable options, and an experience that leaves you feeling pampered and refreshed when you finally reach your destination.

text:
China-based METiS TechBio (HKEX: 7666), an AI-powered drug delivery company, signed up to a research and discovery collaboration deal with US giant Eli Lilly and Company. Under the deal, METiS will apply its AiLNP platform to develop tissue-specific lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery technologies and is eligible for an upfront payment in the low double-digit millions of USD, up to approximately USD 1.1 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestones, and single-digit tiered royalties on annual net sales of resulting products. The collaboration is at the research and discovery stage; no specific targets, indications, or clinical programs are disclosed. ​

AiLNP is METiS's proprietary AI-driven ionizable-lipid discovery and optimization platform, combining generative and predictive AI for rational LNP design to address the challenge of improving LNP targeting and biodistribution for tissue-specific delivery of therapeutic modalities. The company also highlighted its PhatGPT lipid generative model, although it did not specify any targets, indications, or drug candidates covered by the agreement.

The Lilly agreement adds to a series of partnerships signed by METiS in 2026, which listed to the HKEX in May. In June, the company licensed its preclinical trispecific T-cell engager MTS-128 to Boulevard Bio for USD 20 million upfront and up to USD 1.6 billion in milestones. METiS also established collaborations with Deerfield Management, Hengrui Pharma, and Grit Biotechnology, and reported more than RMB 6 billion in aggregate potential transaction value across its OpenCGT drug-delivery partnerships as of May 2026.
