title: Microsoft's Maia 300 swaps raw compute for a 2.5x memory bandwidth gain as it moves to ...
description:
The vehicle of its choice is Maia 300, which Rani Borkar, president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, and Saurabh Dighe, corporate vice president of systems planning and architecture, detail in an architecture deep dive.
Gartner forecast this week that AI providers will spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 alone, and that AI revenue won't cover the build-out profitably until at least 2032.
Whether Maia 300 is the final catalyst for such a move, though, is a harder case to make.
Maia 300 moves from Maia 200's single die to a multi-chiplet package, with compute on TSMC's N2P process and memory-controller and I/O functions split onto separate dies.
The Maia 300 announces something the rest of the industry already knew, albeit more subtly: Custom silicon is no longer a side project for hyperscalers.
text:
Microsoft will make Maia its main inference engine at multi-gigawatt scale, following Google and Amazon into in-house silicon

Microsoft's upcoming Maia 300 trades a modest 36% compute gain for 2.5x Maia 200's memory bandwidth, betting on memory-bound decode, with production in 2027

Hyperscalers supply just over half of Nvidia's data center revenue at a 75% gross margin, so each move to in-house chips affects not only its pricing power but the chip industry's sustainability as a whole

In 2024, Microsoft told the European Commission that Google was the only company vertically integrated at every AI layer, from chips to a mobile app store, and that "everybody else must rely on partnerships to innovate and compete."

Now, it has revealed plans to follow the same route without breaking a sweat.

In an Official Microsoft Blog post, Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Cloud + AI, said Microsoft will scale its Azure Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027 and make Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft's products and services.

The vehicle of its choice is Maia 300, which Rani Borkar, president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, and Saurabh Dighe, corporate vice president of systems planning and architecture, detail in an architecture deep dive.

Feeding the beast, not growing it, as it takes the Google route

The move is a pointed statement from one of Nvidia's biggest customers, and it lands as bubble worries grow louder. Gartner forecast this week that AI providers will spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 alone, and that AI revenue won't cover the build-out profitably until at least 2032.

If the largest buyers of AI hardware stop paying Nvidia's margins for the work they do most, the most richly valued part of that build-out starts to look exposed. Whether Maia 300 is the final catalyst for such a move, though, is a harder case to make.

Maia 300 moves from Maia 200's single die to a multi-chiplet package, with compute on TSMC's N2P process and memory-controller and I/O functions split onto separate dies. Eight HBM4 stacks deliver 288GB at 18TB/s per accelerator, against 216GB at 7.1TB/s for Maia 200, according to StorageReview's breakdown of Microsoft's spec sheet.

Microsoft hasn't abandoned compute so much as rebalanced around memory. In decode, the token-by-token phase that dominates long reasoning chains and agent loops, accelerators spend much of their time waiting on data rather than doing arithmetic.

The Maia 300 tries to close that gap by keeping data near the compute that uses it, through a non-uniform memory layout across chiplets, software-managed on-die SRAM, and narrower number formats, including an enhanced MXFP4 and sub-3-bit storage formats, with hardware conversion between them. The Maia 300 announces something the rest of the industry already knew, albeit more subtly: Custom silicon is no longer a side project for hyperscalers.

Google, the company Microsoft singled out two years ago, began recognizing revenue from TPU system sales delivered to customer data centers in the second quarter, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on Alphabet's July earnings call, while CEO Sundar Pichai said the company is "seeing strong demand for TPUs as standalone systems from other customers."

It isn't the only one either; Anthropic has lined up 3.5GW of TPU capacity through Broadcom for 2027, on top of an earlier deal for up to a million TPUs, and Meta was reported in 2025 to be in talks to rent-cum-purchase them. Amazon has gone the same way. CEO Andy Jassy said in April 2026 that Amazon's chip business, spanning Trainium, Graviton and Nitro, had passed a $20 billion annual revenue run rate and was now "one of the top three data center chip businesses in the world." OpenAI, meanwhile, has lifted the lid on its own Jalapeño accelerator.

Nvidia's margins: the AI holy grail?

The incentive is plain from Nvidia's own results. In the quarter to July 2026, the company reported $96.2 billion in revenue, $89 billion of it from data centers, at a 75% gross margin. CFO Colette Kress put hyperscale revenue at $49 billion on the earnings call, meaning a little over half of Nvidia's data center business comes from a small group of buyers, the biggest of which now design their own accelerators.

Every inference workload that moves in-house is one where that buyer pays closer to manufacturing cost instead of Nvidia's margin. Microsoft told investors in July that Maia 200 was up to 40% cheaper to operate than Nvidia's latest chips on OpenAI and Microsoft models.

It did, however, fail to name a particular GPU it called a "leading GPU-based system," an important distinction given Nvidia's focus on efficiency via Vera Rubin, which OpenAI even refused to compare against outright.

The reveal didn't move stocks much; on Monday, Nvidia shares closed down 1.29% after the reveal, while Microsoft's rose 1.14%, and Microsoft's opaqueness about efficiency gains may be one reason.

The other reason is equally important: Evercore ISI analysts estimate Maia will account for only about 10% of Microsoft's AI chip spending by the first quarter of 2027, CNBC reported, and Nvidia has guided to $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter.

Scale is arguably an ongoing constraint, however; at 167 kW per rack, a gigawatt of rack power is roughly 6,000 Maia 300 racks, or about 575,000 accelerators, before cooling and facility overheads.

Going the Google route hasn't stopped anyone buying from Nvidia either. Amazon, with its "top three" chip business, is still set to take more than 3 million Nvidia GPUs by mid-2028.

Alphabet, which now sells its own TPUs, raised its 2026 capex guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion in July, lists Vera Rubin alongside its own TPUs, and Ashkenazi said it is "still in a supply constraint environment."

Microsoft keeps Nvidia and AMD for training, and Satya Nadella said earlier in 2026 that "because we can vertically integrate doesn't mean we just only vertically integrate."

Jensen Huang's answer to the custom silicon question on Nvidia's August call could have been written about Maia: "Whereas many of these XPUs are inference-specific chips for one cloud or one service, NVIDIA is a platform." Microsoft's counter-bet is somewhat different: one cloud is big enough.

The deeper problem for the pin theory is that custom silicon changes who collects the margin, not how much gets spent. Gartner warns that the industry needs about $8.5 trillion in revenue between 2026 and 2030 to earn a reasonable return on its build-out, versus no more than $3.6 trillion it expects AI to generate. Microsoft isn't responding by building less; it is planning gigawatts more, and cheaper tokens arguably help close that revenue gap rather than widen it.

Some of what Microsoft saves will also flow elsewhere in the supply chain. Maia 300's pitch rests on HBM4, the same constrained memory Nvidia's Rubin uses at the same 288GB per package, and its compute dies come from TSMC, which supplies everyone.

Google's TPUs are developed and supplied under a long-term agreement with Broadcom, whose CEO Hock Tan said that "many investors in AI don't understand what they're putting their money into," and who expects chip shortages to ease only around 2028 or 2029. Nvidia isn't sitting idle either; it already paid $20 billion to license Groq's SRAM decode technology, a sign it sees the same inference threat coming.

Until production silicon ships and someone outside Microsoft can measure it, Maia 300 is a well-argued design whose most important numbers are ones that only Microsoft has seen, and a reminder that the biggest threat to Nvidia's margins may be its best customers rather than its rivals.

title: Commerzbank: UniCredit's Succession Planning, a Neutral Stance, and the Long Road Past 30%
description:
The ECB gave UniCredit permission on Thursday to lift its stake beyond the 30% threshold with no fixed ceiling, a decision the Italian group called an important milestone.
JPMorgan kept its "Neutral" rating on the shares unchanged yesterday, with a price target of 39 euros.
A regulatory green light to expand a shareholding says nothing on its own about Commerzbank's revenue, profit or operating trajectory.
Verdi fears up to 15,000 job losses at Commerzbank, which employs roughly 40,000 full-time staff worldwide.
Ad Commerzbank Stock: New Analysis - 17 October Fresh Commerzbank information released.
text:
UniCredit has reportedly begun scouting potential successors to Commerzbank chief executive Bettina Orlopp and is weighing a broad reshuffle of the German lender's supervisory board, according to Bloomberg. Neither move has been confirmed, and both sit well ahead of any completed takeover — a distinction that matters as much as the headlines themselves.

The personnel chatter lands alongside a regulatory picture that is only partly resolved. The ECB gave UniCredit permission on Thursday to lift its stake beyond the 30% threshold with no fixed ceiling, a decision the Italian group called an important milestone. That clearance does not close the deal. UniCredit expects to wrap up the remaining regulatory procedures around the turn of the year, after which it reckons it could hold roughly 50% of Commerzbank's voting rights and take control. Further approvals remain outstanding, and the European Commission's competition review — with a provisional deadline of 16 November 2026 — is the next concrete checkpoint.

Two Clocks Running at Once

Investors are effectively watching two separate timelines. The first is the ownership question: permission to build the stake, the expected completion of the approval process, and the eventual transfer of control. The second is Commerzbank's own operating performance, which comes into focus on 05.11.2026, when the bank publishes results for the third quarter of 2026.

JPMorgan kept its "Neutral" rating on the shares unchanged yesterday, with a price target of 39 euros. The stock closed at 37.56 euros, below that mark. The confirmation is neither a downgrade nor an upgrade — the US bank trimmed neither its rating nor its target, but the note offers no fresh optimism either. It sets a cautious valuation frame ahead of the quarterly report rather than signalling any re-rating already under way.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Commerzbank?

The two threads should not be conflated. A regulatory green light to expand a shareholding says nothing on its own about Commerzbank's revenue, profit or operating trajectory. By the same token, a quarterly report does not stand in for the steps still pending on the path to a possible takeover. Commerzbank declined to comment on the ECB approval.

What Integration Would Actually Touch

Beyond the shareholding arithmetic, the deal's political dimensions are sharpening. Analysts and supervisors warned in media reports that integrating the two banks could shift credit decisions away from Frankfurt — a prospect that gives extra weight to the German government's demands for commitments on mid-sized corporate lending, the role of Frankfurt and job protection.

No disruption to credit supply has been established. The warnings describe possible consequences of an integration, not a relocation that has already happened. That gap between political demands and binding pledges, and between feared cuts and announced measures, is central to how the transaction should be read.

Employment is the other flashpoint. Verdi fears up to 15,000 job losses at Commerzbank, which employs roughly 40,000 full-time staff worldwide. The union is flagging a risk, not describing an announced reduction.

Commerzbank at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

The Finish Line Is Later Than the Milestone

Even a completed control transfer would not mean the two banks become one. Reuters reports that UniCredit plans full integration only in 2029–2030. Competition conditions, possible management changes and any commitments on mid-sized business lending will shape how much room the Italian group gets to operate — questions the approval to build the stake leaves unanswered.

For shareholders, the practical upshot is a clear separation between the possible acquisition of control and the later operational merger. The stake-building permission answers one question. The rest — personnel, credit policy, and the timing of integration — is still open.

title: In nearly 2 decades of leading philanthropy at the Milken Institute, I've never seen a tidal ... - Fortune
description:
The two leading artificial intelligence labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are both racing to IPO in the coming months, each with estimated valuations of at least $1 trillion.
It’s estimated an additional $37 billion will flow to the philanthropy sector annually.
The question before these tech employees should not be what this wealth can buy, but rather what it can do.
In my nearly two decades of leading strategic philanthropy at the Milken Institute, I have spent ample time with philanthropists, their families, and financial advisors, helping identify how their wealth could be used amid economic booms and busts.
So as this third wave of philanthropy comes to shore, let’s rally around these new philanthropists.
text:
In 2026, the world witnessed the largest initial public offering in history when SpaceX raised $75 billion, achieving a $1.77 trillion valuation. But those massive figures may soon be eclipsed. The two leading artificial intelligence labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are both racing to IPO in the coming months, each with estimated valuations of at least $1 trillion.

The massive valuations of AI labs mean that thousands of tech workers are suddenly becoming wealthy. It’s estimated an additional $37 billion will flow to the philanthropy sector annually. The question before these tech employees should not be what this wealth can buy, but rather what it can do.

In my nearly two decades of leading strategic philanthropy at the Milken Institute, I have spent ample time with philanthropists, their families, and financial advisors, helping identify how their wealth could be used amid economic booms and busts. Just last year, I spent time interviewing several ultra-high-net-worth families as they grappled with how to transition their legacy of giving to the next generation.

What I’ve come to learn is that philanthropic potential has never been greater than it will soon be. In 2026 alone, US charitable giving rose to $617 billion. This new capital only has a track record of exponential growth. If used strategically, it can be leveraged to unlock $1.5 trillion in catalytic capital or guide trillions in annual government funding. Let us embrace this historic moment with some tested principles of wayfinding in philanthropy.

I’d like to address directly those who are set to garner this new, unfounded wealth for the first time. There will be a litany of ways to use this capital. The first step is to establish an identity of how to give that represents your core values. Some of the best philanthropy starts from a place of personal connection.

Next, these new wealth generators must lean into the complexity of today’s most pressing problems – those that feel nearly impossible to solve, such as closing the hunger gap, estimated on the low end of $33B annually, to managing plastic pollution, estimated on the low end of $50B annually. Just as AI now allows us to find connections, patterns, anomalies, and insights more quickly than ever before, that spirit and mindset can be brought to tackling housing insecurity, climate change, poverty, and so many other multifaceted problems. These challenges aren’t solved with single interventions, but rather by systems-based solutions that may require careful choreography of complementary approaches – research, building novel partnerships, policy change, awareness campaigns, social movements, or impact investment into commercial solutions.

Philanthropy can rewire and transform systems. It is society’s risk capital and can be deployed strategically to derisk solutions so other types of funding – from the government to the capital markets – can flow in. Through our work at the Milken Institute, we have seen time and time again the power of philanthropy to derisk – from advancing unproven, early-stage medical research to identifying and testing novel technologies created by entrepreneurs from around the world with no commercial track records – and creating investable opportunities for other financing that can bring pioneering solutions to market and at scale.

The philanthropy journey can be lonely, but there is an opportunity for connections to learn and grow together. Giving circles are the fastest-growing form of philanthropy, having tripled from 2016 to 2023. At the Milken Institute, for example, we have several opportunities for philanthropists of all backgrounds to gather, connect, and meet on a peer level to learn from one another and explore ways to pool resources to achieve maximum charitable impact. This is a welcome opportunity to invite this new cohort into the fold.

There is a perception that philanthropy is outdated. That it is solely about garnering positive press, and that nonprofits are not equipped to drive the change we need. However, true philanthropy, as I’ve come to know, is not as simple as writing a check, but when done with intention, can lead to real-life, impactful change.

The exact timeline for when these AI companies go public is still in flux, but there is no doubt that new wealth will be coming online soon, and some of it is already here. This is a call to action for this new cohort of captains to continue the legacy set before them by decades of philanthropists. This could be one of the largest infusions of new philanthropic capital in a generation. It must not go to waste. The seas are too stormy, and the stakes are too high.

So as this third wave of philanthropy comes to shore, let’s rally around these new philanthropists. May they find their North Star, set off with the courage and curiosity of our history’s greatest explorers, embrace the unknown and unimaginable, and find out not just where they can go, or what they can buy, but what they can do to make the world a better place.

title: Volvo bets on Nvidia for eyes-off driving, minus the lidar - AutoNext
description:
Tesla's FSD has held Dutch approval since April 2026 The Dutch RDW approved Tesla's FSD Supervised on 10 April 2026, the first approval of its kind in the European Union, and has since pushed for the same system to be cleared across the EU.
Klaus Zellmer will most likely launch the first Hyperion Volvo The first Nvidia Hyperion Volvo will most likely reach showrooms under Klaus Zellmer, who joins from Skoda as chief executive on 1 October 2027.
AutoNext Take Volvo spent 2022 telling buyers that unsupervised driving needed lidar on every car, then removed the lidar in 2025 to save money.
Hyperion lets it promise eyes-off driving again on cameras and radar, with lidar as an add-on.
The first Hyperion Volvo will be named, with its markets, before Zellmer arrives in October 2027; any later, and a launch due before 2030 slides into the next decade.
text:
Nvidia's Alpamayo software runs two driving stacks at once

Nvidia's Alpamayo stack runs an AI reasoning model and a conventional camera-and-radar perception system at the same time, each acting as a check on the other. Ali Kani, who heads Nvidia's automotive division, says the combination deals with stop signs, traffic lights and unprotected left turns without the driver stepping in, and that the open-source Alpamayo models have been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers. Nvidia calls the result Level 2++, a grade that appears nowhere on the SAE's six-step scale, so the driver stays legally responsible throughout. The first hardware set carries no lidar, although Hyperion has room for one.

Volvo once ordered 1.1 million Luminar lidar sensors

Volvo's 2020 contract with Luminar covered 39,500 lidar sensors, a figure raised to 673,000 in 2021 and to 1.1 million in 2022. All of it was built around the EX90 and Ride Pilot, the unsupervised motorway mode Volvo announced in January 2022 with California as its launch market. Ride Pilot never reached a customer. In September 2025 Volvo made lidar optional on the EX90 and shelved it on future models to save cost, a decision that cut Luminar's expected lifetime volume by about 90 percent, according to Luminar's own bankruptcy filings. Luminar entered Chapter 11 in December 2025.

EX90 owners already received a free Nvidia computer swap

Every electric Volvo on sale today runs on Nvidia's Orin chip, and the two companies have worked together since 2017. Owners of early EX90s were offered a free replacement of the car's core computer with the twin-Orin unit fitted to the ES90, so that their cars could run the features Volvo had planned for them. Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo's head of software development, now says the company will standardise more on Hyperion, sensor set included. He also says the technology will reach plug-in hybrids and petrol models as well as electric cars.

Tesla's FSD has held Dutch approval since April 2026

The Dutch RDW approved Tesla's FSD Supervised on 10 April 2026, the first approval of its kind in the European Union, and has since pushed for the same system to be cleared across the EU. Volvo's current Pilot Assist still needs clear lane markings and combines adaptive cruise control, steering support, lane-change assistance and curve speed adaptation. The planned Nvidia-based system works much like Tesla's FSD Supervised and Rivian's Universal Hands-Free, both of which already run on customer cars. A Volvo arriving late in the decade would join them at least four years after Tesla's Dutch approval.

Klaus Zellmer will most likely launch the first Hyperion Volvo

The first Nvidia Hyperion Volvo will most likely reach showrooms under Klaus Zellmer, who joins from Skoda as chief executive on 1 October 2027. Håkan Samuelsson signed the agreement, and Bakkenes says the debut model is a brand-new car that will come in the "not-too-near future". Neither company disclosed the value of the deal or named the model. Volvo sold just over 710,000 cars in 2025, 46 percent of them electrified, and its EX60 ramp-up is running well behind plan, which suggests the self-driving budget is competing with more immediate problems.

AutoNext Take

Volvo spent 2022 telling buyers that unsupervised driving needed lidar on every car, then removed the lidar in 2025 to save money. Hyperion lets it promise eyes-off driving again on cameras and radar, with lidar as an add-on. That looks like a sound engineering call, and it also means the reasoning behind each unprotected left turn in a future Volvo will be Nvidia's code rather than Volvo's.

The first Hyperion Volvo will be named, with its markets, before Zellmer arrives in October 2027; any later, and a launch due before 2030 slides into the next decade. If Tesla's FSD wins EU-wide approval first, Europe's best-known safety brand will be selling supervised driving years after Tesla, on the one subject Volvo has always claimed as its own.

text:
UniCredit has cleared the single most symbolic regulatory barrier in its pursuit of Commerzbank. The ECB's Thursday authorization allows the Italian lender to push past the 30% stake threshold and build its holding without any fixed cap. What it does not do is complete a takeover — and the gap between permission and possession is where the real story sits.

That distinction matters because a second, entirely separate conversation is unfolding alongside it. JPMorgan confirmed its "Neutral" rating on Commerzbank yesterday, holding its price target at €39. Neither an upgrade nor a downgrade, the note offers no fresh optimism; the shares closed at €37.56, below the target but with no buy recommendation attached. Two questions — UniCredit's creeping control and Commerzbank's own operating performance — are running on parallel clocks, and investors would be wise not to blur them.

A timetable stretching to the end of the decade

According to Il Messaggero, UniCredit envisions a reorganization of Commerzbank followed by a later merger with HypoVereinsbank. An extraordinary shareholder meeting is expected in early 2027, no later than February, with full integration projected for 2029–2030. UniCredit itself expects to satisfy the remaining regulatory conditions around the turn of the year, after which it aims to hold roughly 50% of voting rights and thereby secure control. The ECB nod is a prerequisite for that build-up — not a substitute for the outstanding procedures and offer conditions.

The next hard date on the calendar is 16 November 2026, when EU competition authorities are due to rule. Polish approval is anticipated before year-end, per the same report.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Commerzbank?

Berlin wants guarantees, and Verdi is counting jobs

Political resistance has not faded. Kathimerini reports that the German government is demanding commitments on the stock exchange listing, the Frankfurt headquarters, employment levels, and the supply of credit to small and medium-sized enterprises — conditions that touch the very architecture of any combined group. Verdi, meanwhile, fears up to 15,000 job cuts at Commerzbank, a figure that lays bare the tension between integration economics and workforce interests.

The 2030 profit test

For the combined entity, Il Messaggero cites estimates of around €21 billion in profit and roughly €45 billion in revenue for 2030. Those are projections for a planned union, not results in hand. They set the bar against which the industrial logic of the deal will be judged — and that bar is not the only one in play.

Bettina Orlopp had already raised Commerzbank's standalone ambition: a profit of just under €6 billion for 2030, up from a prior plan of just under €5 billion. Any merger case must therefore clear a higher independent hurdle than existed before. A larger group, on its own, does not answer whether it creates more value than the bank could deliver alone.

Commerzbank at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

What actually gets tested next

Commerzbank publishes third-quarter 2026 results on 5 November 2026 — the next scheduled checkpoint for the operating side of the ledger. A regulatory green light says nothing about revenue, earnings, or business momentum; a quarterly report, conversely, does not advance the pending steps toward control. Commerzbank declined to comment on the ECB authorization.

For shareholders, the binding items ahead are concrete: the outstanding approvals, the specific terms of integration, and how UniCredit intends to reconcile its reorganization blueprint with Commerzbank's upgraded standalone targets. Until those land, the stock sits between a permission and a completion — with a neutral analyst, a €39 target, and a date in November to keep it company.

title: Oobit Lets AI Assistants Pay with Stablecoins Via One-Time Cards | The Fintech Times
description:
Oobit, a Singapore-based stablecoin payments firm, has launched Oobit AI Payments, a product that lets users authorise AI assistants to make purchases on their behalf using stablecoins, without granting those assistants access to the underlying account balance or primary payment credentials.
When a user asks an AI assistant to book, buy or pay for something, the assistant flags the transaction for approval.
Once the user confirms, Oobit generates a one-time virtual card tied exclusively to that transaction.
The AI receives the card details it needs to complete checkout; it never holds the user’s wallet credentials or sees the broader account.
The one-time card model is not new in isolation.
text:
Oobit, a Singapore-based stablecoin payments firm, has launched Oobit AI Payments, a product that lets users authorise AI assistants to make purchases on their behalf using stablecoins, without granting those assistants access to the underlying account balance or primary payment credentials.

The mechanism works through ephemeral card issuance. When a user asks an AI assistant to book, buy or pay for something, the assistant flags the transaction for approval. Once the user confirms, Oobit generates a one-time virtual card tied exclusively to that transaction. The AI receives the card details it needs to complete checkout; it never holds the user’s wallet credentials or sees the broader account. Oobit then handles identity verification, authorisation and payment execution in the background.

The product supports USDT and other stablecoins. Users in supported markets can also fund their Oobit balance through local payment rails, including bank transfers, mobile money networks and Brazil’s Pix instant payment system. The company says the solution is available across more than 75 countries.

“AI can already understand what you want and figure out how to get it,” said Amram Adar, co-founder and CEO of Oobit. “The missing piece is the ability to pay. That shouldn’t depend on where you live or which bank card you have.”

The architecture of delegated payments

Oobit’s core design choice, separating permission to pay from access to money, addresses a genuine structural problem in agentic AI commerce. As large language model platforms move from information retrieval into task execution, the question of how an AI agent interacts with financial accounts becomes a live compliance and consumer-protection issue. Unrestricted wallet access creates risks around unauthorised transactions, account takeover and liability attribution that neither banks nor regulators have fully resolved.

The one-time card model is not new in isolation. Virtual card infrastructure has been used in accounts-payable automation, B2B procurement and travel expense management for years. What Oobit is doing is applying that architecture to the consumer-facing AI agent context and running it on top of stablecoin settlement rather than traditional card rails. Whether the underlying settlement is genuinely on-chain or whether Oobit abstracts that into a fiat-equivalent flow for the merchant is not specified in the announcement.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Several payments and crypto firms are positioning for agentic commerce. Visa and Mastercard have both signalled interest in credentialing AI agents for payment execution, while a number of crypto-native firms are exploring stablecoin-based payment APIs for developer integration. Oobit’s differentiation appears to rest on its cross-border reach through local payment rails and its focus on users whose funds originate in digital assets rather than bank accounts.

The regulatory landscape is still forming. In the EU, the revised Payment Services Directive (PSD3) and the accompanying Payment Services Regulation will tighten requirements around delegated payment access and strong customer authentication, which is directly relevant to any model where a third-party agent initiates transactions. In the UK, the FCA‘s ongoing work on payments supervision similarly touches on authorised access and fraud liability. Oobit will need to demonstrate how its per-transaction approval model satisfies authentication standards across the jurisdictions it serves.

text:
In 2014, when Satya Nadella became Microsoft CEO, the company struggled to keep up with a rapidly changing technology sector. He transformed the company's culture with three words: “learn-it-all”, not “know-it-all.” Nadella sought to change how employees approached learning, collaboration and innovation at the technology giant. Drawing on psychologist Carol Dweck's research on growth mindset, he encouraged employees to embrace curiosity, acknowledge what they didn't know, and continuously improve their skills. The shift moved the focus away from proving existing expertise towards learning from others and adapting to change. Nadella repeatedly used the phrase and incorporated the philosophy into management evaluations, making curiosity an important part of Microsoft's workplace culture. More than a decade later, he continues to emphasise learning as the company navigates changes driven by artificial intelligence, while maintaining that its future depends on adapting to new technologies and customer needs.

How three words changed Microsoft's workplace culture

When Nadella became CEO, Microsoft struggled to regain traction in an industry increasingly defined by cloud computing and new technology platforms. He thought a culture that already knew the answers could kill experimentation and inhibit employees from adapting to changing circumstances. The “learn-it-all” approach encouraged employees to ask questions, share knowledge and treat mistakes as opportunities to improve. Rather than viewing uncertainty as a weakness, employees were encouraged to approach unfamiliar problems with curiosity. The philosophy drew on Carol Dweck's growth-mindset research, which distinguishes between believing abilities are fixed and viewing them as qualities that can develop through effort and learning.

Satya Nadella says learning remains central to Microsoft's future

In a recent communication to employees, Nadella reiterated the importance of growth mindset as Microsoft enters another phase of technological change."Growth mindset has served us well over the last decade—the everyday practice of being a learn-it-all, not a know-it-all," he wrote. "It has reshaped our culture and helped us lead with greater humility and empathy. We need to keep that." He also admitted transformation can bring uncertainty, especially as teams restructure and responsibilities move around. His message came as Microsoft cut jobs even as it continued to pour money into infrastructure and artificial intelligence. Nadella described the company's next phase as a process of “unlearning” and “learning,” requiring employees to maintain existing businesses while developing new products, categories and business models.

AI transformation brings a new challenge

Nadella has outlined three business priorities for Microsoft: security, quality and AI transformation. He said the company must continue strengthening its existing products while rethinking its technology infrastructure, platforms and applications for AI workloads. He also described a broader shift in Microsoft's mission, from building software for specific tasks to creating tools that let people and organisations develop their own solutions. The approach reflects Microsoft's efforts to integrate AI across its products and services while building the computing infrastructure required to support them.

Why the growth mindset still matters

Nadella’s focus on learning reflects his view that a company’s long-term relevance depends on its ability to change, not just on what it has already done. In his message to employees, he wrote, "What we’ve learned over the past five decades is that success is not about longevity. It’s about relevance. Our future won’t be defined by what we’ve built before, but by what we empower others to build now." The principle that helped reshape Microsoft's workplace culture remains central to how Nadella wants the company to respond to AI. As technology changes how people work and build products, the “learn-it-all” mindset remains a framework for encouraging employees to learn, experiment, and adapt. ​

Benjamin Chemla, chief executive and co-founder of Shares Group, will lead the enlarged entity.

text:
Shares has completed the acquisition of 100% of Treezor from Société Générale, the companies confirmed on 7 October 2026. The deal creates a combined group with regulatory licences covering electronic money, payment services, investment services and crypto-assets, supervised by the French ACPR and the AMF.

Benjamin Chemla, chief executive and co-founder of Shares Group, will lead the enlarged entity. Treezor will be run by Cédric Cassini, supported by Julien Mortuaire. The transaction price was not disclosed.

What each side brings

Treezor, founded in 2016 and authorised as an electronic money institution by the ACPR, has processed more than €145 billion in transaction volume and issued over 8.5 million cards since inception. It holds principal membership of both Mastercard and Visa, and its regulatory passport covers 25 EU member states. The company already generates close to 70% of its revenue growth outside France, with on-the-ground operations in Germany, Italy and Spain.

Shares began in 2021 as a retail investing application before expanding its regulated technology to serve wealth managers, financial institutions and employee savings providers. It has raised $90 million in total funding from Valar Ventures, Singular, Global Founders Capital and Red Sea Ventures, and employs around 150 people across France, the UK and Poland. Shares Financial Assets holds an ACPR-authorised investment firm licence and is registered as a crypto-asset service provider under both the ACPR and the AMF.

Together the group intends to offer a modular, white-label infrastructure stack that covers the full spectrum from current accounts and card issuance through to savings products and investment portfolios, delivered via API to fintechs, corporates and financial institutions.

“Transforming financial services in Europe requires infrastructure capable of covering the entire value chain, from accounts through to investment. This is the infrastructure we will now build together,” said Chemla.

Market context and competitive read-across

The deal lands at a meaningful moment for European Banking-as-a-Service. The first wave of BaaS providers built their businesses on accounts, cards and SEPA payments, but the commercial ceiling on that model has become visible: margins on commodity payment flows are thin, and several established platforms have faced regulatory scrutiny over the governance of their client onboarding and AML controls. The pressure is pushing the more ambitious players to either deepen their product set or consolidate with complementary capabilities.

Combining payment infrastructure with investment and savings rails is not a common move. Most BaaS providers partner with a wealthtech or savings platform through an API integration rather than bringing both inside a single regulatory perimeter. Shares and Treezor are betting that owning the full stack reduces friction for institutional clients and creates a stickier, higher-value relationship than a point-solution sale.

The regulatory dimension matters here too. Operating under MiCA for crypto-asset services, DORA for operational resilience, and MiFID II for investment products simultaneously is a compliance overhead that smaller entrants struggle to carry. For clients such as banks, insurers and large fintechs that need a fully licensed and auditable partner, that multi-licence position could be a genuine differentiator.

The near-term milestones to watch are the pace at which the combined product catalogue is unified, whether Treezor’s existing institutional clients adopt the investment and savings modules, and whether the group pursues further European licences or acquires additional capabilities to extend its geographic reach beyond its current four-country footprint.

text:
Week of Friday October 16, 2026

1. Anthropic’s Compute & Financial mega-AI IPO Prep: Anthropic did a financial industry show and tell for its financial growth, and AI Compute Infrastructure investments ahead. At an investor day in San Francisco, Anthropic said third-quarter revenue rose nearly 50% to $16.8 billion, its second adjusted profitable quarter in a row, cash-flow positive, with $1.70 of revenue for every $1 of compute. But growth is slowing after the second quarter more than doubled, and some investors now talk of about $1.5 trillion for the IPO, down from about $2 trillion. On the supply side, Anthropic has signed some $530 billion of leases toward 15 gigawatts of capacity, with neoclouds and former bitcoin miners racing to build it, and every month a site like its new Louisiana campus comes online early could be worth over $1.3 billion in revenue. My take, from ARD #186: this is exactly what you are supposed to do before an IPO, balance expectations on both ends, as we did when I ran Goldman’s internet research in the nineties. The growth is still up and to the right; the slower pace will shape the IPO price more than the case for the build. More here.

2. OpenAI’s Ad Revenue efforts back on: OpenAI is back on track with its ad revenue ramp, now up to a billion dollars on tens of thousands of advertisers. Advertisers on ChatGPT jumped to about 60,000 in early October, from 20,000 in late August, and a click costs about $5, versus $30 to $50 on Google. About 140 people now work on ads, nearly half hired since July, with Meta the biggest source of talent. Ads hit a $1 billion annual pace in August, still small next to OpenAI’s nearly $50 billion overall, and the team has reorganized seven times since February, so OpenAI may miss the $2.4 billion 2026 ad target it gave investors. My take, from ARD #185: OpenAI is doing what it takes, all of it at once, from AI coding and the enterprise to AI agents with Dots, and now ads again, a side quest it set aside to focus on Anthropic. With about 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users, and less than 5% paying, much of the rest will be ad driven, the way Google and Meta were built. Slow and steady progress, ahead of its IPO, now pushed to early next year. More here and here.

3. Meta launches its Wonder Frontier AI Models: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang took a victory lap with the launch of its near-frontier Muse Wonder AI models. Trained at Meta’s gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder Full scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind only Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 58, and ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Fable 5.1, all at 53. Meta built it for personal agents, with ‘Active Memory’ and ‘Active Focus’, though it costs more per task than OpenAI’s and Google’s models. Days later, Meta went open too, with Muse Spark Open, which runs locally on Apple’s Mac Studios, as I noted on ARD #185. My take: kudos to Zuckerberg and Wang, fourteen months from a ‘complete talent reboot’ to the frontier. Memory and focus are what mainstream users will feel, far more than benchmark points. But, as The Information notes, everyone now claims the frontier, and users are trading down to cheaper ‘good enough’ models. Today’s frontier is where next year’s ‘good enough’ models come from. More here.

4. Microsoft Copilot aims for ‘Costco of AI’ strategy: Possible Satya Nadella successor and current Copilot chief Charles Lamanna is breathing new life into Microsoft’s AI strategies. In 2025, Lamanna pushed Nadella to pay Anthropic to make Copilot better, which was ‘heresy’ at the time, and moved Copilot off what he calls ‘model monogamy’. Copilot’s corporate users have more than doubled this year to over 30 million, a model router now picks the cheapest model that can do the job, and Microsoft is on track to pay Anthropic over $2 billion a year. And this week Microsoft showed its own 2.8 trillion parameter MAI-Base-2, built on its own data, joining Meta and Nvidia with open-weight options to China’s models, as I discussed on ARD #186. My take: Microsoft under Nadella remains the exception to the rule that incumbents get overrun by a new tech wave. It adjusted, from one model to a model mix, and now competes on value with a bundle. But every task routed to someone else’s model is a cost, not a margin, and the frontier labs sell their own agents to the same customers. More here.

5. Google’s Gemini 4 Argon back at frontier: Google scrambled back to the frontier with its latest Google Gemini 4 Argon model. It is Google’s first major frontier release since Gemini 3 late last year, and Google says it beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 on coding, science, finance and law. Independent tests are less generous: the Artificial Analysis Index has Argon at 53, tied with Astra, behind Opus 5.5 and Meta’s Muse Wonder Full, as I laid out in AI-RTZ #1238. Google is pricing to win, at about a fifth of Astra and Fable for now, and it landed a day after Meta’s Wonder. Two frontier launches in two days. My take, from ARD #183: expect frontier leadership to keep ebbing and flowing, in an infinite game, not a race. Google is unique, with a full vertical stack from chips to billions of users, so it can afford to arrive late, and cheap. Its core goal is still ‘good enough’ models for the billions, as I said in ARD #175, while Argon tells enterprises it can still go neck and neck at the frontier. More here.

Additional Items.

text:
Dive Brief:

Southwest Airlines is adding a new tier and enhanced perks to its Rapid Rewards loyalty program, the airline announced Thursday.

Starting in January, Southwest’s current tiers, A-List and A-List Preferred, will change to Silver and Gold, respectively. The carrier is adding a Platinum tier, which will sit above Silver and Gold.

Among the perks for platinum tier members is an unlimited companion pass, which allows members to travel with one friend or family member, and make changes to who that individual is up to three times a year.

Dive Insight:

Southwest has overhauled its Rapid Rewards program in an effort to provide more valuable rewards while still making it easy to earn points, according to Nandika Suri, VP of Rapid Rewards at Southwest Airlines.

“As our Members engage more with Southwest, they’ve told us they want Rapid Rewards to reward them in more meaningful ways, whether they’re working toward status or using the points they’ve earned,” Suri said in a prepared statement. “These updates build on that feedback by rewarding Members throughout their Southwest experience, while keeping the simplicity and value that have always set our program apart.”

The program has seen massive growth in 2026, with membership in the second quarter increasing 35% year over year to nearly 100 million members.

Southwest has been working on expanding Rapid Rewards’ appeal to a broader audience and improving its balance of transactional and experiential benefits to drive engagement, Suri told CX Dive during a DiveLive event in August.

The airline has expanded the ways members can redeem points. Starting in the spring of 2027, Rapid Rewards members will be able to earn and use points for international travel via new airline partnerships with Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways.

In November, loyalty members can use their rapid rewards for rental cars with participating car rental providers, and at some point in 2027, members will also be able to use points toward seat selection.

To reach Silver status, Rapid Rewards members must earn 35,000 points or 15 qualifying flights; to reach Gold, members must earn 65,000 points or 50 qualifying flights; to reach Platinum, members must earn 140,000 points or 100 qualifying flights. Starting in January, Rapid Rewards Cardmembers will earn one tier-qualifying point per every $1 spent on purchases.

As one of the market's most closely watched technology companies, NVIDIA also features among the 10 Most Active Blue Chip Stocks to Buy Right Now.

Support Must Earn Its Subscription Fee

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) benefits from CUDA programming tools that make switching platforms costly. Paid subscriptions offer supported software, security updates, and help avoid downtime, creating a route from customer dependence to recurring profits.

Mission Control schedules workloads and automates recovery, helping customers use expensive systems more efficiently. AI Enterprise lists at $4,500 per GPU annually. However, free alternatives exist, and selected GPUs include five-year licenses. Separate renewals must add customer spending beyond bundled hardware purchases and cover engineering and support costs before the installed base deserves a software valuation premium.

The Earnings Forecast Still Rests on Hardware

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) trades at 25x forward P/E, versus 29x trailing reported earnings. That forward valuation looks attractive, supported by second-quarter revenue growth of 106% and management's $108 billion third-quarter revenue outlook. Analysts expect NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) to increase adjusted EPS from $9.31 in fiscal 2027 to $15.91 in fiscal 2028, approximately 71%. Management expects gross margin to ease from 75% to 74% next quarter. Strong sales must therefore offset some margin pressure. Subscriptions could help, but reported results remain dominated by data-center demand.

A Cheaper Multiple Carries Bigger Commitments

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) carried forward P/E multiples of 30x in 2024 and in 2025. Today's lower headline multiple accompanies greater established earnings and cash generation, alongside larger commitments.

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) generated $69.9 billion of first-half free cash flow, while supply and capacity commitments reached $279 billion across future years. Delayed customer deployments could leave inventory consuming cash and expose margins to write-downs. June's $25 billion debt issuance adds financing costs.

Subscription renewals could diversify those economics, but the company does not separately disclose these products' recurring revenue or renewal rates. Investors should demand recurring cash after reinvestment before assigning them material value.

The Closest Rival Requires More Earnings Catch-Up

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) carries a 25x forward P/E against 39x for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), its closest listed AI-accelerator rival. Analysts forecast adjusted EPS growth of approximately 107% for the rival in 2027, versus 71% for the company's fiscal year ending January 2028. These periods largely cover the same calendar year.

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) also earns much higher operating margins: approximately 66% under GAAP in its latest quarter versus 17% for the rival, whose PC and embedded businesses broaden its mix. First-half free cash flow represented roughly 39% of sales versus 19% for the rival. Company-adjusted earnings now include stock compensation, while the rival excludes it.

Faster expected peer growth supports some valuation premium, but the profitability and cash-conversion gaps make the discount attractive. Slower growth could still support the valuation if margins and collections hold up; simultaneous weakness would erode that cushion. For most active blue chip stocks, software growth must ultimately become cash.

Conclusion

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) looks attractively valued, supported primarily by hardware demand. Paid software could improve resilience if renewals add profit after support costs. Sustained sales growth, margins near guidance, and disciplined inventory conversion support that judgment. text:
Mercedes was the first vehicle manufacturer to receive Level 3 autonomous driving approval in Europe, but there are still a lot of limitations to the functionality. For instance, the vehicle equipped with such ADAS can only reach speeds of up to 95 km/h and only on certain highways. Mercedes calls it Driver Pilot, and it was developed in collaboration with Nvidia. Today, the two companies announced that they are extending their partnership and will continue to work on a next-generation autonomous driving system.

Mercedes provided the expertise when it comes to safety and integration. At the same time, Nvidia brought the technology: Nvidia Hyperion is the in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture, and Nvidia Alpamayo Stack is the driving software with AI reasoning capabilities. Nvidia Halos is the safety system providing redundancy and guardrails.

The aim is to bring an SAE-Level 4 system that handles the entire driving task on its own and responds to problems in a timely manner, within certain operating conditions. This eliminates the need for a human to take over control. It's a step below Level 5, which is essentially full automation without any restrictions on roads and conditions.

Mercedes and Nvidia also highlight that we will see deeper integration between Mercedes' MB.OS and Nvidia's Hyperion system.

text:
In this monthly roundup, leadership changes across the global beauty and personal care industry reflect an increasing emphasis on operational efficiency, financial discipline, digital transformation and international growth. From boardroom appointments and executive succession to legal oversight and emerging retail channels, companies are strengthening their leadership teams to navigate an increasingly complex commercial environment while positioning their businesses for long-term success.

Operational leadership is taking centre stage at some of the industry’s largest luxury and beauty groups. LVMH appointed Alexandre Oulès as Chief Operating Officer of its Beauty Division, reinforcing the importance of operational excellence as the group continues to develop its fragrance and cosmetics portfolio. The appointment reflects the growing need for coordinated management across global brands, manufacturing operations and international distribution networks.

Financial leadership is also undergoing change. Coty appointed Soraya Benchikh as Chief Financial Officer amid its ongoing business transformation, placing new leadership behind financial strategy as the company seeks to improve performance and strengthen its operating model. The appointment highlights the increasingly important role of finance executives in managing restructuring, capital allocation and long-term profitability.

Corporate transformation is driving leadership changes elsewhere. Oriflame appointed Kenneth Benaim Campbell as CEO, marking a new chapter for the beauty and wellness company as it continues to navigate changing market conditions and evolve its business model. The appointment places fresh leadership behind efforts to strengthen commercial performance and support future growth.

Boardroom expertise remains another priority. Ulta Beauty appointed Brieane Olson, CEO of PacSun, to its Board of Directors, bringing experience in retail, consumer engagement and brand development. As beauty retailers compete for younger consumers and adapt to evolving shopping habits, expertise from adjacent retail sectors is becoming increasingly valuable.

Legal and regulatory leadership is also receiving greater attention. Johnson & Johnson appointed Aviva Wein as Global Vice President of Litigation, strengthening its senior legal team as the company continues to manage complex legal matters. Meanwhile, Kimberly-Clark appointed Suzana Blades as General Counsel ahead of its planned acquisition of Kenvue, reinforcing the importance of legal oversight and corporate governance during major transactions.

Leadership succession is shaping the strategic direction of global consumer goods companies. Procter & Gamble (P&G) appointed Shailesh Jejurikar as Chairman following its leadership transition, marking another significant step in the evolution of the group’s executive structure. The move highlights the importance of continuity and long-term planning as multinational businesses navigate changing consumer demand and competitive pressures.

At L’Oréal, the appointment of Rahquel Purcell as North America DE&I Chief reflects the group’s continued investment in organisational leadership and workplace strategy. As global beauty businesses operate across increasingly diverse markets, leadership structures are evolving to address talent development, inclusion and corporate culture alongside commercial performance.

Digital commerce is creating new leadership requirements. Nykaa appointed a former Instamart executive to lead its quick commerce expansion, demonstrating how India’s beauty retail market is adapting to growing consumer expectations around convenience and rapid delivery. The appointment reflects the increasing overlap between traditional beauty retail, ecommerce and on-demand fulfilment as companies seek to capture new purchasing occasions.

Brand communications also remain central to competitive positioning. The Estée Lauder Companies appointed Madeleine Boyd to lead global brand communications, strengthening its ability to manage brand storytelling and consumer engagement across international markets. As beauty brands navigate a fragmented media environment, strategic communications leadership is becoming increasingly important to maintaining relevance and protecting brand equity.

Taken together, this monthly roundup demonstrates that executive appointments are increasingly being shaped by the strategic challenges facing the beauty and personal care industry. Operational efficiency, financial transformation, legal governance, digital commerce and brand communications are all influencing leadership decisions. In 2026, the companies best positioned for long-term growth will be those that combine experienced leadership with the flexibility to respond to changing markets, technologies and consumer expectations.

title: 'It will be us': Former Australian of the Year is building her answer to OpenAI - SMH
description:
A former Australian of the Year is establishing what she calls a world-first atomic-scale chip plant in Sydney in a bid to make her company Australia’s answer to OpenAI.
“We are establishing an atomic-scale manufacturing plant in Sydney.
It’s the first one in the world,” she told the audience at the Commonwealth Bank’s Sydney offices.
Those quantum states are fragile, and no company has yet built a quantum computer that can correct its own errors at a useful scale.
Watermelon is not a full quantum computer.
text:
A former Australian of the Year is establishing what she calls a world-first atomic-scale chip plant in Sydney in a bid to make her company Australia’s answer to OpenAI.

Michelle Simmons, founder and chief executive of Silicon Quantum Computing, was asked at the John Monash Foundation oration on Thursday evening whether Australia could produce a quantum equivalent of OpenAI or Anthropic. “Yes, it will be us,” she said.

“We are establishing an atomic-scale manufacturing plant in Sydney. It’s the first one in the world,” she told the audience at the Commonwealth Bank’s Sydney offices.

An SQC spokesman said the company was expanding its manufacturing with “a new facility to be announced”, but would not say where it would be, when it would open or what it would cost.

Ordinary computer chips store information as ones and zeros. Quantum computers store it in the quantum states of individual atoms or particles, which in theory lets them solve problems beyond any conventional machine, such as simulating molecules to design new drugs, batteries and materials. Those quantum states are fragile, and no company has yet built a quantum computer that can correct its own errors at a useful scale.

SQC makes its chips by placing individual phosphorus atoms in silicon, a technique Simmons and her team spent 25 years developing at UNSW.

The federal government’s $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund has put $60 million into SQC this year, alongside London venture firm Firgun Ventures and Tin Alley Ventures. The spokesman said that money had “played a key role” in the new facility.

The plant comes as SQC’s first product, a chip called Watermelon, starts to find buyers. Watermelon is not a full quantum computer. It works alongside conventional AI models to sharpen their predictions, and Simmons said tests with energy multinational Schneider Electric had improved the accuracy of next-day energy network forecasts by an average of 20 per cent.

She said Watermelon had five paying customers: Schneider, Telstra, the Commonwealth Bank, the Defence Department and a high-frequency trading firm that has not been announced.

CBA and Telstra are both early investors in SQC. A CBA spokesman described the bank’s use more cautiously, saying it had been experimenting with the chip “to see where the technology might be of benefit”.

Simmons said demand was outstripping what SQC could make. “Since the announcements of both Telstra and Schneider, we have literally tens of customers trying to get in there,” she said. “The challenge we’ve got now is how to make more of that product quickly so we can get it out into the hands of more customers.”

She said SQC was standing by its target of a full, error-correcting quantum computer by 2033. The company has modelled its timeline on conventional computing, which took from the first transistor in 1947 to the arrival of personal computers in the early 1980s. SQC built its first single-atom transistor in 2012.

“The error-corrected processor, the 2033, is the 1981 equivalent,” Simmons said. “I’m standing by that because I’m pretty confident on that, but I’m hoping we’ll get it sooner.”

She said the new plant would make Sydney “the home of atomic-scale manufacturing”, and that much of its supply chain was already in Australia.

The oration is the annual dinner of the General Sir John Monash Foundation, which since 2001 has awarded $41.1 million in scholarships to 300 Australians to study at leading overseas universities.

Hugo Rourke, a former scholar who studied at Harvard on a CBA-funded scholarship and is now chief financial officer of health company Navigator Group, said the government too often compared Australia with countries such as France and Britain, when the real competition for founders was the US.

“It’s pretty clear that most founders in Australia go to the US,” he said. “If France is our competitor for talent, then we’re not shaping up the way we need to.”

Rourke said Sydney property prices were part of the problem. “If you leave university today and you want to buy a house in Sydney, it is incredibly attractive to go and stick in a professional services firm and make money as fast as possible,” he said.

Simmons said talent was also flowing the other way, with about 70 per cent of SQC’s staff coming from overseas, increasingly from the US. “Australia is a great place to be to build companies,” she said.

David Swan moderated a fireside chat at the event, which was hosted by the Commonwealth Bank, an investor in Silicon Quantum Computing.

text:
Asia-Pacific medical technology (MedTech) demand is expected to reach US$132 billion (S$170.9 billion) by 2030, growing at 6.9 per cent annually — outpacing the global market growth rate of 5.5 per cent over the same period1. Capturing this opportunity requires clinical evidence, capital, clear regulatory pathways and manufacturing partners.

Singapore has built an ecosystem that brings these critical enablers together, helping MedTech companies scale and succeed. We are home to the world’s top 30 MedTech companies, with the sector generating over S$20 billion in manufacturing output and employing more than 17,000 people.

Here is how Singapore's ecosystem helps companies innovate and scale globally.

1. Research and clinical partnerships that speed up product development

WHY IT MATTERS: Building a globally competitive MedTech product rarely follows a straight line from lab to market. As then Minister-in-Charge of Energy and Science & Technology, Dr Tan See Leng noted at the Singapore Medical Device Venture Showcase in June 2026, a commercially viable MedTech business needs more than good science – other factors like regulatory clarity, patient capital, manufacturing capabilities, industry partnerships and talent matter, too."2

HOW SINGAPORE HELPS:

Productisation support: MedTech Catapult, a S$38 million national platform under the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), helps MedTech companies bridge the gap between research and market adoption. It brings together engineering and prototyping capabilities with quality assurance, clinical, regulatory and business development expertise to de-risk product development and accelerate commercialisation.

Connections with research and clinical partners: Global companies can work with hospitals, universities and research institutes on product development and clinical research. Agilent, for example, established the US$29 million (S$38.6 million) National University of Singapore-Agilent Hub for Translation & Capture to develop new ways of translating clinical research into diagnostics. Singapore also offers sustained public investment in biomedical and translational research under the S$37 billion Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2030 plan.

Growing access to capital and venture support: Investors and venture-building platforms including ClavystBio, Santé Accel Singapore, and SG Growth Capital provide healthcare ventures with capital, mentorship and global networks.

PROOF IN PRACTICE:

EssilorLuxottica: Its Singapore Centre for Innovation & Technologies Asia helped conceptualise the Stellest® lens with the company’s other R&D hubs globally, manufactured prototypes for clinical trials in the United States and China, and led clinical studies and programme coordination. In 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration authorised Stellest® as the first spectacle lens to slow myopia progression in children.

Bypass Solutions: Working with MedTech Catapult and local contract manufacturers, it has completed key preclinical studies for its peripheral artery disease treatment and is moving towards a first-in-human trial in Singapore.

2.Regulatory credibility that can cut time to market

WHY IT MATTERS: Asia is a high-growth but fragmented market. Each jurisdiction retains approval authority, so repeated regulatory reviews consume time and capital.

At the LSI Asia Emerging MedTech Summit 2026, Adjunct Professor (Dr) Raymond Chua, Chief Executive Officer of Singapore's Health Sciences Authority (HSA), pointed to HSA's growing network of regulatory reliance arrangements as a way to reduce duplication — making Singapore an increasingly practical entry point for companies looking to move efficiently from one approval to many across the region.

name: Microsoft
title: British watchdog seeks tougher terms around Microsoft's dominance of business software
description:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications.
Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades.
Rivals back licensing scrutiny Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds.
The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK.
In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions.
text:
The UK's competition watchdog wants to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in business software, allowing the regulator it to intervene to level the playing field, and says it is considering other areas for investigation.

Regulators around the world are watching to see what the UK decides in this case, with bodies such as the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the European Commission mulling similar actions.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications.

This follows an investigation the regulator started back in May into Microsoft’s software portfolio including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, plus its security, server and operating systems. The watchdog is also probing whether Microsoft enjoys a position of “substantial and entrenched market power” through the suite of software that could be seen as stifling competition and harming buyer choice.

It lays out its proposed decision in a document [PDF] and is inviting comments that must be submitted by November 13. The CMA will make its final decision by February 13, 2027.

Bargain spotter

The CMA makes it clear the company holds a strong position in each of the five areas it investigated (personal computer operating systems, productivity software suites, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems), and that customers face barriers when switching providers – limiting their choice and weakening the ability of other software developers to offer rival products.

Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades. It finds that many customers view Microsoft's portfolio as a unified software environment, forming an end-to-end, integrated stack which makes for easier technical integration between products, with discounted pricing for buying whole bundles of applications together.

This makes customers less likely to adopt products from alternative providers that may offer similar or superior functionality, as doing so would duplicate licensing costs for products already in their Microsoft bundle, the CMA says.

“Organizations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives,” said CMA chief exec Sarah Cardell.

Finding that the criteria for SMS designation are met would not imply or assume wrongdoing on Microsoft’s part, the regulator stresses.

A separate document [PDF] spells out the potential interventions that the CMA could make. These include ensuring that Microsoft’s technical design choices do not restrict the ability to use other providers; that commercial arrangements (like bundling) do not limit effective competition; and preventing Microsoft from using its market power in business software to distort competition in adjacent activities, such as cloud services.

Rivals back licensing scrutiny

Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds.

The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK. This largely fizzled out with the watchdog securing undertakings from Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) that they would work to reduce barriers to switching between clouds and operating multi-cloud deployments.

In an update, the CMA says that more can be done to address barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services, and it will continue to work with AWS and Microsoft to address them.

It also says it its looking into whether customers can freely choose the best AI tools, and whether alternative AI providers have a level playing field to compete against Copilot.

In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions.

“All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition,” a spokesperson told us.

However, some pressure groups were quick to signal their approval. The Browser Choice Alliance said it welcomes the CMA’s proposed decision, adding that: “BCA members have long experienced how Microsoft leverages its market power from Windows and productivity software to push users towards its Edge browser, even where they’re trying to use an alternative.”

The Open Cloud Coalition, which counts Google as a member, said: “Microsoft’s restrictive software licensing practices distort competition in the cloud, harm choice, and increase costs. This once-in-a-generation opportunity to end these practices can strengthen competition and lower customer costs, if the CMA acts quickly and decisively.” ®

At Microsoft and GitHub, I watched senior leaders get 60 to 70 pages of status updates every week. Nobody reads that. Leaders skim for problems, and the real ones get buried under update after update that says “on track” followed by three paragraphs explaining everything that’s going on. And don't get me started about "watermelon status" updates. So I built an AI skill that turns the context from people's day-to-day work into a rollup a leader can read in under a minute. It was inspired by a workflow in Agentic Beyond Code, and it sorts every piece of work into four buckets: 🚨 Needs help: health dropped, dates slipped, or it’s off track 👋 Needs a nudge: nobody has updated it in over a week 🎉 Worth celebrating: shipped this week or on track for weeks straight ✅ Everything else: one line with a count The pattern works with any tool that tracks status and history. I built this version in Productboard Spark and scheduled it to run every Monday, so leaders get it without anyone writing it. If you want the skill, reach out and I’ll send it your way. Would love to hear if other leaders have flipped status updates from pushing lots of paper to pulling what they need to enforce the values of the org.

Transcript

Hi, I'm Chris Butler and I'm a product evangelist for product board. One of the things I dealt with a lot whenever I would help senior leaders in a product OPS role was to help them understand what was going on inside their teams and where they could potentially intervene or help out. And when I was working at Microsoft and GitHub, one of the biggest problems for a senior vice president was that they might get something like 60 or 70 pages worth of these types of updates every week from the all the teams that they had reporting into them. And so I started to think about like, how might we make it easier to go from a push of status to these? Leaders to them, being able to pull it out of the environment. Using product board Spark, I created a skill to be able to get a leader a weekly rollup of things that they should take action on. And for this weekly rollup I want to get some information about initiative that is happening right now. And so the skill is now going to grab everything that's associated with this initiative, look for changes in status, look for comments, and then start to build a roll up for me. And so now the report is coming back with some key information. It's trying to show me where I might need to intervene or kind of pre escalate before the team asks for help. Maybe some places where something hasn't been updated for a while that need me to give it a nudge. And then one of the things I think is most important actually for building kind of cultural values within an organization is really finding places where you can celebrate people and the work they've done. And then of course, it tries to hide anything that is not actually that valuable for me to get update about. And now the great thing about this is that I can take the skill and create some type of schedule, say I want to be able to do this on some weekly basis, say every Monday after people have filled out their status on Fridays. And so with that, if you're interested in the skill and want to check it out, either go to the Makers community or I will be posting this.
