text:
The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.

The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.

Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.

Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.

Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.

The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips.

“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”

Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.

On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access.

The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year.

“It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said.

Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay.

“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

text:
L’Oréal Travel Retail has partnered with global travel experience retailer Avolta to scale sustainability practices and refillable fragrance formats at its international travel hubs.

The French beauty giant’s travel retail arm has formalised a joint Sustainability-Linked Business Plan with Avolta, which focuses on expanding refillable beauty formats, lowering supply chain emissions and scaling circular solutions at travel hubs.

This operational roadmap is targeting 10% in refill solutions by 2030 across L’Oréal’s core fragrance categories.

This is in response to market data, cited by L’Oréal Travel Retail, which shows that 80% of Gen Z shoppers are looking for sustainable beauty products in Duty Free.

Tickets are now available for the 25th anniversary of the Pure Beauty Awards, taking place on 15 October 2026 at the Grosvenor House Hotel in London, UK. Join the beauty industry for an evening of recognition and celebration as this year’s winners are revealed. Click here to secure your place.

The Sustainability-Linked Business Plan will also see L’Oréal Travel Retail work to lower transport-related impact through low emission transport modes and optimised truckload capacity.

Dedicated Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) training modules will also be rolled out for frontline beauty advisors at its international travel hubs.

"Together with Avolta, we are translating shared sustainability commitments into measurable operational steps, expanding refillable beauty and lowering our logistics footprint across key travel hubs,” said Eva Yu, President, L’Oréal Travel Retail.

Avolta is a global travel experience retailer which operates across airports, motorways, cruises and rail hubs.

The company combines travel retail and food and beverage (F&B).

L’Oréal Travel Retail signed the Sustainability-Linked Business Plan agreement with Avolta at TFWA World Exhibition & Conference 2026 in Cannes, France, a global summit for the duty-free and travel retail industry.

Image caption: Eva Yu, President of L’Oréal Travel Retail, and Nicolas Girotto, Chief Commercial Officer at Avolta, presenting the joint Sustainability-Linked Business Plan at TFWA World Exhibition & Conference.

text:
Albertsons Companies has withdrawn its fiscal 2026 outlook as it conducts an operational review following lower second-quarter profit and falling identical sales.

The US food and drug retailer will withhold updated forecasts until the review concludes in its fourth quarter, when it plans to present refreshed financial frameworks alongside a turnaround plan.

In its first quarter, it had forecast identical sales between -1.5% and -0.5%, adjusted EBITDA of $3.55bn to $3.62bn and adjusted net income per Class A common share of $1.75 to $1.85.

The ongoing examination covers customer strategy, cost structures, operating models, banner portfolios, market assets, and capital allocation priorities.

It follows the ACI Edge programme launched in July 2026, which consolidated 11 divisions into four regions and centralised centre-store merchandising under a single team.

For the second quarter ended 12 September 2026, net income fell 69.4% to $51.5m, and diluted earnings per share dropped to $0.11 from $0.30.

Adjusted net income declined 27.9% to $179m, with adjusted earnings per share decreasing to $0.36 from $0.44.

Operating income fell to $174.5m from $295.3m, whilst adjusted EBITDA declined to $784m from $848.4m.

Net sales and other revenue dropped to $18.89bn from $18.91bn, driven by a 0.8% decrease in identical sales.

Digital sales grew 11%, whilst higher fuel takings and pharmacy revenue – despite headwinds from the Inflation Reduction Act – partially offset the top-line reduction.

Gross margin narrowed to 26.8% from 27% due to digital delivery and handling costs alongside higher shrink, partly offset by improved pharmacy margins.

Cost management offset operating inflation and merger litigation costs, while store impairments and equipment disposals lifted property disposition losses to $42.4m from $4.4m.

First-half net sales reached $43.83bn, compared with $43.79bn a year earlier, but operating income fell to $438.1m from $744.6m, and net income dropped to $136.2m from $404.9m.

Capital expenditure reached $899.6m, funding 38 remodels, seven store openings, and digital investments.

As of 12 September 2026, the company operated 2,240 stores, including 1,709 pharmacies and 408 fuel centres.

Albertsons CEO Susan Morris said: "We are launching a comprehensive business review to speed up improvements in Albertsons' performance and tackle even harder a cost structure we can no longer afford. Our work will find opportunities to simplify the organisation, improve decision-making, reinvest savings in customer value, and boost long-term shareholder returns."

text:
The agreement marks an important step in the industrial roll-out of Perpetual Next’s Biomethanol Blueprint, a standardised concept designed to enable the serial development and replication of large scale biomethanol facilities based on proven industrial technologies.

Under the Agreement, Air Liquide Engineering and Technologies will provide its RectisolTM and LurgiTM Methanol technology. The technology is designed to process syngas from a broad range of sources, including syngas from biomass and has been deployed in numerous industrial plants worldwide.

Perpetual Next’s Blueprint integrates torrefaction, gasification, syngas cleaning and upgrade, with methanol synthesis to convert low-grade organic waste, including waste wood, into biomethanol. The standardised approach is intended to reduce development complexity, support repeatable project execution and create economies of scale across a portfolio of facilities.

Perpetual Next is developing its biomethanol portfolio to address growing demand for renewable carbon-based methanol in the chemical industry and maritime sector. Its Delfzijl facility in the Netherlands is planned with a planned biomethanol production capacity of 220 000 tpy, while the company’s broader global development pipeline is intended to create significant production capacity through replication of the Blueprint.

Rolf Bosma, Managing Director, Perpetual Next: “This suite of agreements marks an important milestone in the industrialisation of our Biomethanol Blueprint. Delfzijl will be the first application of the concept, providing the foundation for subsequent projects in Moerdijk, Poland, Estonia and other sites worldwide. By establishing a framework with Air Liquide for multiple biomethanol sites, we are creating a scalable technology platform that supports the roll-out of our biomethanol portfolio.”

The agreement combines Perpetual Next’s standardised project concept and feedstock strategy with Air Liquide’s established technology and engineering capabilities, providing a platform for the development of multiple industrial-scale biomethanol facilities.

name: Eli Lilly
title: Roche Puts Up $100M to Pursue Promising But Competitive New Target in Obesity
description:
It’s the latest in a series of Roche business deals to build up the company’s metabolic drug pipeline.
This different approach offers the potential for use as a standalone treatment or in combination with established obesity drugs.
The Carmot drugs address GLP-1 and GIP receptors, the same targets as Lilly and Novo’s obesity drugs.
With the Rona drug, Roche joins a growing group of companies testing siRNA therapies in obesity.
Last month, the company began a Phase 2a study testing WVE-007 in combination with the Lilly obesity drug Zepbound.
text:
For Roche to catch up to Eli Lilly and Novo in metabolic medicines, it needs its drugs to offer differentiation from those rivals. Roche might have just found a way, agreeing to pay $100 million to license a contender that brings a different modality to a new obesity target.

The drug comes from Shanghai-based Rona Therapeutics. According to deal terms announced Tuesday, Roche gains global rights to the molecule, whose name was not disclosed. It’s the latest in a series of Roche business deals to build up the company’s metabolic drug pipeline.

Formed in 2021, Rona develops RNA interference (RNAi) drugs, an approach that uses small interfering RNA (siRNA) to degrade messenger RNA, interfering with the translation of a disease-driving protein. This approach is sometimes called “gene silencing.” RNAi drugs first reached patients as treatments for liver disorders, but the field has been working to expand the modality beyond the liver. Roche’s new drug comes from a Rona platform technology that enables extrahepatic drug delivery. Rona also claims its therapies offer the potential to be best in class with longer duration, deep knockdown of target proteins, and improved tolerability.

The Rona pipeline lists two obesity drug, both in preclinical development for undisclosed targets. The target of Roche’s newly licensed drug is activin receptor-like kinase 7 (ALK7), a protein that is primarily expressed in fat cells. ALK7 plays a role in a signaling pathway that regulates fat storage, the breakdown of stored fats, and the balance of the intake and expenditure of energy.

Rona points to genetic studies showing that reducing ALK7 activity is associated with favorable results in fat distribution and metabolic measures. Unlike the currently available peptide drugs designed to mimic gut hormones to affect appetite and energy intake, Ronas say ALK7 inhibition acts directly on the biology of fat tissue. This different approach offers the potential for use as a standalone treatment or in combination with established obesity drugs.

“Obesity represents a significant health challenge that requires differentiated treatment options for patients,” Boris Zaïtra, Roche head of corporate business development, said in a prepared statement. “We are excited to partner with Rona Therapeutics, complementing our robust [cardiovascular, renal & metabolic disease] pipeline and reinforcing our commitment to delivering next-generation metabolic therapies.”

Roche jumped into obesity drug R&D with the $2.7 billion acquisition of Carmot Therapeutics in 2024. The Carmot drugs address GLP-1 and GIP receptors, the same targets as Lilly and Novo’s obesity drugs. Last year, Roche began a partnership on petrelintide, a Zealand Pharma peptide designed to activate the receptor for amylin, a hormone key to regulating blood sugar and appetite. One goal for petrelintide is reducing fat in a way that does not also lead to muscle loss, a known problem for obesity drugs. Roche added yet another approach to obesity in August, licensing a Hanmi Pharmaceutical peptide designed to activate CRF2 receptors to reduce fat and increase muscle mass.

With the Rona drug, Roche joins a growing group of companies testing siRNA therapies in obesity. Wave Life Sciences’ siRNA drug WVE-007 goes after a different but related target. It’s designed to silence INHBE, the gene that provides the instructions for activin E, a liver-secreted protein that activates ALK7. Wave has said WVE-007 is intended to stimulate the breakdown of fat while preserving muscle. Late last year, Wave announced preliminary Phase 1 results that it said support once- or twice-yearly dosing. Last month, the company began a Phase 2a study testing WVE-007 in combination with the Lilly obesity drug Zepbound.

GSK joined the ALK7 chase in May, licensing rights to Suzhou Siran Biotechnology’s SA030, a long-acting siRNA in development for metabolic and vascular diseases. The deal calls for SiranBio to complete the ongoing Phase 1 study. After that, GSK will be responsible for further development of the drug outside of Greater China.

Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals has two siRNA therapies in development for obesity: the ALK7-targeting drug ARO-ALK7 and the INHBE gene-silencing therapy ARO-INHBE. Both are in Phase 1/2a testing. Meanwhile, RNAi therapies pioneer Alnylam Pharmaceuticals has an INHBE-targeting siRNA drug in preclinical development for obesity.

Biotech company iBio takes yet another approach with IBIO-610, an antibody designed to block activin E. In July, iBio reported results in monkey tests showing a single dose achieved near complete inhibition of the target protein through eight weeks. These results also showed fat loss and muscle preservation.

The $100 million that Roche agreed to pay Rona consists of an upfront and near-term milestone payments. Rona could receive up to $1.06 billion more if the drug achieves milestones, plus royalties from sales if it reaches the market.

For Agilent, that cooperation runs in both directions — global technologies help meet Chinese customers' needs, while insights from China inform products and solutions for international markets.

text:
Stronger local capabilities and steadier China-US ties could support innovation worldwide by connecting China's research and manufacturing strengths with global expertise, a senior executive of a United States-based technology company said.

Jonah Kirkwood, senior vice-president and chief commercial officer at Agilent Technologies, a California-headquartered company in analytical and clinical laboratory technology, said China's skilled workforce, extensive supply chains and readiness to adopt new technologies further underpin its commitment to the market.

"Today, China is both an important market for us and an integral part of our global supply chain, manufacturing and innovation network," Kirkwood said.

According to the company, the Chinese market delivered 9 percent year-on-year revenue growth on a core basis in the quarter ended July 31, driven by double-digit growth in pharmaceutical and food markets.

"A more stable bilateral relationship would give us greater confidence to advance long-term collaboration," Kirkwood added, calling for sustained dialogue to create a more transparent and predictable business environment.

Greater policy certainty and smoother movement of people and commerce would help companies plan long-term investments and allow researchers and businesses in both countries to work together on shared challenges, he said.

For Agilent, that cooperation runs in both directions — global technologies help meet Chinese customers' needs, while insights from China inform products and solutions for international markets.

Within the company, Chinese customers are increasingly helping define research problems and develop solutions, Kirkwood said, with their needs feeding into global product plans.

"This means that China is an important market for applying advanced technologies and also a source of customer insight, engineering experience and innovative ideas that can inspire our global solution development," he said.

The senior executive sees that contribution in laboratories seeking to integrate artificial intelligence into experimental design, data analysis and daily operations, moving beyond purchases of individual instruments.

"Chinese customers' emphasis on real-world application, together with their ability to test, iterate and scale new technologies quickly, makes China an important window into the future of laboratory development," he said.

Agilent's partnership with Chinese technology company Purspec offers another example. The partners combined Purspec's lipidomics hardware, software and databases with Agilent's chromatography and mass spectrometry platforms to develop a solution for studying lipid structures.

During the project, Chinese researchers contributed original technologies and knowledge of emerging scientific needs, while Agilent brought instrumentation and an international market network.

"These collaborations reinforce my confidence that China can contribute a wealth of original scientific achievements, engineering capabilities and application insights," Kirkwood said.

Looking forward, Kirkwood sees particular promise in China-US cooperation in areas such as life sciences and biopharmaceuticals, food and environmental safety, green energy and laboratory digitalization, where progress depends on scientists, companies and customers working across borders.

"Enduring collaboration often begins with a specific challenge," he said, adding that translating positive momentum from high-level dialogue into lasting outcomes requires companies to pursue open innovation, invest in local capabilities and build long-term trust with customers, suppliers, research institutions and industry partners.

Agilent plans to put that approach into practice by deepening local manufacturing and research collaboration in China over the next two to three years, Kirkwood noted.

text:
Collaboration will bring together NVIDIA AI technologies and Danaher's scientific instruments, laboratory workflows and data

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Danaher Corporation (NYSE: DHR) today announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of scientific discovery. As part of Danaher's broader effort to shape the future of AI-enabled science, the companies are working to combine Danaher's scientific instrumentation, automation technologies, laboratory workflow software and domain expertise with NVIDIA accelerated computing and AI technologies. The goal is to help researchers move faster from prediction to experimental evidence, creating a continuous learning cycle where experiments inform models and models help design better experiments.

"AI is reshaping how science is conducted, and Danaher is at the forefront of that transformation," said Julie Sawyer Montgomery, President and Chief Executive Officer of Danaher. "We are collaborating around a shared vision for more connected, adaptive and accessible innovation, helping researchers solve consequential challenges and translate discovery into human impact."

"The next era of scientific discovery will be driven by a continuous loop between AI and experimentation," said Kimberly Powell, Vice President of Healthcare at NVIDIA. "Together with Danaher, we are bringing accelerated computing and physical AI into the lab - connecting models with instruments and real experimental data, where experiments improve models and models design better experiments, helping researchers compress years of discovery into months."

Danaher and NVIDIA are working to integrate AI into scientific instruments through edge computing like NVIDIA DGX Spark, accelerated analytics and data processing with RAPIDS, real-time inference, scientific reasoning and foundation model technologies, including BioNeMo Open Models. Initial efforts focus on a select group of priority instruments, with the potential to expand across a broader portfolio over time. The companies are exploring how scientific and physical AI, such as NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Omniverse Digital Twins, can support more intelligent instruments and laboratory workflows, while keeping experimental evidence at the center of scientific decision-making.

The collaboration seeks to advance Danaher's commitment to connected science by bringing AI, accelerated computing, instruments, workflows and experimental data together to produce experimental evidence. Danaher aims to help researchers reduce the time and complexity of moving from an AI-generated prediction to the experimental evidence needed to act on it, while preserving customer choice in models, standards and technology providers.

text:
Whilst the global spotlight remains fixed on the power struggle between the United States and China for dominance in artificial intelligence, France is building its own digital sovereignty. This is no longer merely a matter of political ambitions proclaimed in European forums, but of large-scale industrial implementation that is bringing agentic computing – artificial intelligence systems capable of acting autonomously, without constant human supervision – directly into the vital nerve centres of the real economy. The picture that emerges is that of an ecosystem spanning the entire value chain, from hardware to applications, yet one in which there remains a single key supplier. This marks a significant shift, recently documented on NVIDIA’s official blog, demonstrating how the seeds sown during the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the ‘Choose France’ summits are generating a tangible return on investment.

Strategic independence depends on the ability to process data in-house and control the physical infrastructure. It is in this context that Bull’s expansion of AI server production in Europe should be viewed; from 2028, the company will manufacture systems based on the powerful NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 architecture directly at its newly opened plant in Angers. The concept of the ‘sovereign vault’ also extends to intangible data. The CANUT framework agreement, for example, has made Twake.ai (based on the NVIDIA Nemotron model) the only certified digital workspace for over 2,500 French public bodies, managed by LINAGORA and Docaposte. Meanwhile, in the financial sector, the operator SBS is creating secure platforms that will enable banks to develop generative AI services whilst keeping data strictly within their own corporate boundaries – a non-negotiable requirement for credit institutions.

If hardware is the security perimeter, software is the competitive driving force behind this French revolution in technological infrastructure. Here, France is playing the open-source card, with Mistral AI (which has just released its Large 4 model) leading the way. But it is the application in the real economy that is truly surprising. The most fascinating example comes from the space economy. The Altair-1 satellite, successfully launched this month (the result of integration with Loft Orbital), literally takes AI into orbit. Thanks to the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin modules and Mistral models, the satellite is capable of performing real-time Earth observation processing and autonomous operations directly in space, bypassing the traditional – and slow – transfer of data to the ground.Even the traditional manufacturing and cosmetics industries are reaping a competitive advantage. L’Oréal has integrated the NVIDIA ALCHEMI architecture for in silico research: by combining computational simulations with laboratory experimentation, the cosmetics giant has accelerated the process of discovering new active ingredients by up to a hundred times, demonstrating that AI does not replace traditional research but exponentially multiplies its efficiency. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila are managing around 5,800 kilometres of roads and buildings using a digital twin-based agent, achieving a 10 per cent reduction in operating costs, with a target of 30 per cent once fully operational. Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, which enables employees to build agents in a controlled environment. In the field of quantum computing, Alice & Bob and Quandela are integrating the NVQLink platform to connect GPUs and quantum processors.

The ‘French model’ provides clear evidence that the technological drive towards sovereignty does not end with the purchase of advanced semiconductors. It requires an integrated ecosystem where the state’s vision (with its catalysts) is seamlessly integrated with private infrastructure, academic excellence and national software leaders. This is a crucial lesson for Italia – which is currently seeking to chart its own path to digital sovereignty – and for Europe as a whole. text:
What You Should Know

Analytical and clinical laboratory technology giant Agilent Technologies Inc. announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire digital pathology software and AI company Proscia®.

Transaction financial terms: an all-cash acquisition valued at $240M in cash at closing, plus up to an additional $30M contingent on achieving future operational and financial performance milestones (total potential deal value of $270M).

Closes the loop on a four-year commercial partnership: Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-market an open digital diagnostic pathology ecosystem.

Unifies an end-to-end precision medicine triad: merges Agilent’s established portfolio of automated slide stainers, pathology instrumentation, diagnostic reagents, and companion diagnostics (CDx) with Proscia’s vendor-agnostic enterprise software platform, Concentriq®, which serves as an operational orchestration layer across scanners, LIS networks, and AI algorithms.

Assembling the Full Pathology Stack

By acquiring Proscia, Agilent secures the missing software operating system. Instead of selling discrete instruments and reagents, Agilent can now deliver an end-to-end ecosystem: tissue preparation reagents, automated staining instrumentation, vendor-neutral whole-slide ingestion, and regulatory-cleared diagnostic software.

Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-develop and sell integrated diagnostic pathology workflows. Acquiring Proscia transitions an external commercial alliance into an owned intellectual property core.

Agilent is a primary diagnostic partner for global pharma, co-developing FDA-approved companion diagnostic tests that determine patient eligibility for targeted cancer immunotherapies. Integrating Concentriq gives Agilent a direct digital data conduit into 16 of the top 20 biopharmas, creating an R&D feedback loop that unites prospective biomarker discovery with downstream clinical commercialization.

Transaction Economics & Target Operating Benchmarks

The acquisition brings a high-margin, recurring-revenue software foundation into Agilent’s diagnostic portfolio:

Valuation Multiple & Purchase Price: Agilent is deploying $240M in cash at closing plus up to $30M in earnouts against Proscia’s trailing twelve months (TTM) revenue exceeding $18M —representing an upfront enterprise value-to-revenue multiple of approximately 13.3x (expanding to 15.0x including full earnouts), reflecting high market demand for enterprise software operating layers in diagnostics.

Commercial Scale and Penetration: Proscia’s platform—anchored by its flagship Concentriq® software—is deployed across more than 4,000 laboratories, hospital systems, and clinics across North America and Europe.

Top-Tier Biopharma Validation: Proscia software currently supports translational research and trial operations for 16 of the top 20 global pharmaceutical companies.

Clinical Performance Benchmarks: Proscia earned 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology (securing the highest vendor performance score across both U.S. and European markets) and holds U.S. FDA 510(k) clearance for primary clinical diagnosis.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Padraig McDonnell, President and CEO of Agilent. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data.”

Taylor Farms has indefinitely suspended sourcing iceberg lettuce from central Mexico during certain months of the year following a summer cyclosporiasis outbreak that sickened thousands across multiple states.

In an Oct. 8 letter to consumers, Founder and CEO Bruce Taylor said the company will stop harvesting and processing lettuce for sale in the U.S. or Canada during the Cyclospora season defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The CDC designates the period as May 1 through Aug. 31, which Taylor said mirrors central Mexico’s rainy season.

Nevertheless, the fresh-food processor remained at the center of the FDA’s outbreak probe. Besides suspending harvesting in central Mexico for four months each year, Taylor Farms plans to expand year-round health monitoring and increase irrigation water and crop testing in the region, Taylor said. The company also plans to lead and invest in research and technology to improve tools for detecting and preventing Cyclospora.

The company will also participate in a public-private task force that includes the FDA, scientists, industry leaders and public health officials, Taylor said. The group’s mandate includes identifying prevention measures for fresh produce growers.

text:
By Sanskriti Shekhar

Oct 13 (Reuters) – Albertsons withdrew its fiscal 2026 forecasts on Tuesday and launched a review of its business aimed at cutting costs, lowering prices and reversing sluggish sales.

The US grocer has battled cautious consumer spending, particularly ​by lower-income shoppers, as food and fuel costs climb, alongside market share ‌loss to mass retailers such as Walmart, discount chains and private-label brands.

The review builds on a restructuring, announced in July, and is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter ending February 2027.

By then, Albertsons also aims to provide fresh short- and long-term financial targets alongside a “comprehensive turnaround plan”.

“We must turn ‌things ​around,” Meg Whitman, the former eBay and Hewlett-Packard CEO ⁠who was named executive chair last ⁠month in a newly created role to help the grocer “sharpen its strategy and strengthen execution”, said on a post-earnings call.

The company needs to move faster to cut costs and reinvest much of those savings to lower prices and improve store ​experience, she said.

CEO Susan Morris said Albertsons had accumulated too many initiatives, processes and layers of complexity over time, slowing the organization and increasing costs.

“We’re not satisfied with ⁠the results and the current trajectory of our ⁠business,” she said.

The expanded turnaround effort comes nearly two years after ​Albertsons’ proposed $24.6 billion merger with Kroger collapsed after a federal court blocked the deal on ​antitrust grounds. Albertsons subsequently terminated the agreement.

The company’s shares rose 2% on ‌Tuesday, reversing premarket losses. They had fallen 27% so far this year.

“They have hard time remaining competitive on price as some mass merchants such as Walmart have used grocery as a traffic driver and have other high margin categories such as fashion to offset ⁠food’s low margins,” said Bruce Winder, an independent retail consultant.

In July, Albertsons outlined plans to expand private-label offerings and improve e-commerce, while restructuring its 11 divisions into four regions and ⁠centralizing merchandising.

Albertsons on Tuesday described ‌those changes as the first step in its broader turnaround.

“We’ll ⁠exit areas that are underperforming,” Morris said on Tuesday.

Albertsons in July ​forecast fiscal ‌2026 adjusted earnings per share in the range of $1.75 to $1.85 ​and projected ⁠annual identical sales to decline in the range of 0.5% to 1.5% after trimming its annual target.

The grocer on Tuesday reported that its same-store sales in the second quarter ended September 12 fell 0.8%.

But adjusted profit of 36 cents per share beat estimate of 33 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

(Reporting by Sanskriti Shekhar in Bengaluru; Editing by Sahal ​Muhammed and Sriraj Kalluvila)

Q & A Highlights

Q: Mark Carden (UBS) asked why now is the right time to announce a comprehensive business review, coming right after ACI Edge, and how the updated approach impacts ACI Edge's ramp and scope.A: CEO Susan Morris explained this is an evolution of ACI Edge, aimed at moving faster and more aggressively. While Q2 met expectations, the pace of improvement hasn't been fast enough to translate into sales, share growth, traffic, and earnings. She acknowledged that too many initiatives over the last 18 months created complexity and competing priorities. Going forward, focus will be on three things: driving customer experience, improving financial performance, and aggressively removing cost and complexity. Initiatives not aligned with these will be paused or stopped, with a more comprehensive plan to come at the Q4 earnings call.

Q: Edward Kelly (Wells Fargo) asked how much more room there is on cost savings given the sizable cost cuts already underway, and how the company balances speed of change with associated risk, particularly regarding the philosophy of savings versus upfront investment.A: CEO Susan Morris stated there is still substantial "blue sky" in cost-out across three areas: cost of goods (via Buying Better Together), goods not for resale (aggregating demand of an $80 billion company), and SG&A (more headcount reduction expected in the next 12-18 months). She also cited store conditions, including shrink and waste management. On speed, she emphasized that focus on fewer initiatives will drive stronger results faster, balancing risk against conflicting priorities. Interim CFO Cody Perdue added there is a lot more room to run on the cost side at a more accelerated pace to fund investment.

Q: Leah Jordan (Goldman Sachs) asked about the level of inflation seen in the business during the quarter, transportation expense trends, supplier feedback, and how inflation should trend in the back half of the year.A: CEO Susan Morris reported CPI picked up to about 2.5% in Q2, while the company passed along less than that, roughly 2% to 2.1%. Interim CFO Cody Perdue added that suppliers are coming with some cost increases, and the company has a playbook to handle them. Inflation is being seen across the P&L, but this is not new, and they will continue to manage these headwinds.

Q: Simeon Gutman (Morgan Stanley) asked for perspective on pricing position nationally and locally, and any progress since Susan took over.A: CEO Susan Morris said the approach is surgical, looking at pricing market by market, category by category, and item by item, as opportunities vary across the country. Last year, the company engaged in three price campaigns with strong success. They are learning from those pilots to understand what drove faster unit and profitability inflection, and will make strategic investments as part of the larger plan to be discussed in Q4.

Q: Rupesh Parikh (Oppenheimer) asked for puts and takes on the top line for the back half of the year, including headwinds like IRA and Cyclospora, and whether the company can quantify them.A: Interim CFO Cody Perdue unpacked the headline ID sales of minus 0.8%, noting pharmacy was up low to mid-single digits, leaving the core down just over 1.5%. He said nothing has fundamentally changed from the Q2 exit rate. The 30-basis point Cyclospora impact and 30 basis points of egg deflation are considered cyclical, not structural headwinds.

Q: John Heinbockel (Guggenheim) asked about value perception versus reality and the speed with which the company can improve value perception, noting it requires significant investment and aggressive marketing in chosen markets.A: CEO Susan Morris said value perception is a blend of product quality, variety, services, ease of shopping, and price. The goal is not to be the cheapest but to have the right balanced value proposition by market. Price investments will be surgical and strategic by market and category, not broad-based reductions. The approach is methodical and data-driven, with more details to come in Q4.

Q: Tom Palmer (JPMorgan) asked for an update on the CFO search and whether Board changes and the comprehensive review affect the timeline or candidate profile.A: CEO Susan Morris said the CFO search is underway and making good progress. She believes the evolving Board shape is exciting and that having Meg Whitman onboard sends a strong signal of support. She is confident they will find the right fitsomeone aggressive, who wants to drive change and help shape strategy. She is very optimistic about the search.

Q: Robbie Ohmes (Bank of America) asked about owned brands and whether to expect an acceleration in efforts, and about the balance between promotions versus tightening price spreads and SKU rationalization.A: CEO Susan Morris confirmed the company is absolutely accelerating owned brands efforts, improving variety, quality, and cost. On pricing versus promotions, she said it's a balance with surgical frontline pricing changes by market and category, and a refined promotional strategy. On SKU rationalization, the company is optimistic about growing owned brand share and aggressively pursuing cost reductions while carrying the products customers want and being efficient from a labor perspective.

Q: Kelly Bania (BMO) asked for a specific update on the Buying Better Together program, including the percent of national buying on the program and how savings are coming in, and whether the business review might cause a rethink or pause.A: CEO Susan Morris said the company is centralizing center store and has clearly communicated this to vendor partners. Negotiations have begun with the largest suppliers to secure lower frontline cost of goods and refine promotional strategy. She does not believe potential portfolio exits would be large enough to dramatically impact vendor negotiations, so it does not weigh into that decision at this moment.
